div.head: TO THE ELECTORS OF THE PARLIAMENTARY DIVISION OF MID-OIEESIIIRE.
div.p: TO THE ELECTORS OF THE PARLIAMEN- TARY DIVISION OF MID-OIEESIIIRE.
GENTLEMEN,—The accession of your senior member to the Peerage has caused a vacmcy in the Representa- tion of this Division. •
Rhe Council of the Liberal Association of Mid- Cheshire has done me the honour to select me as a fitting candidate, and I consequently venture to ask for your support.

My opinions are so well known to you that I need not trouble you by stating them at any length. I am prepared to give a general and independent support to the present Government, believing it to be the best and most Liberal Government that has ever ruled over this kingdom, though I would reserve to myself the liberty, should the occasion arise, of differing from it on the details of any measure.

The programme for the session, as announced in the Queen's Speech, promises much useful legislation. The principles of Local and Municipal Government are to be settled; our Elections are to be made less expensive' and more pure, and a Bill to provide legislative com- pensation for unexhausted improvements by the tenant farmer is to be introduced. I am convinced that no Bill on this subject will be adequate that does not contain provision that no tenant should leave his farm without full payment for what he has expended In raising its letting value, and which he has not got back; that no sitting tenant should have his rent raised upon his own Improvements; and that there should be full freedom of sale and culture. 1 would most earnestly support a Bill containing these provisions, and feel sure that they may be carried out without infrirging the rights of the owners of the soil.
I believe also that the present law of agriciOural distraint is indefensible and is as injurious to the tradesman as it Is oppressive to the occupier.

I should rejoice to see in the Municipal and County Government Bill power given to the representatives of the ratepayers to deal with the question of licenses. Those who have to pay the bills for the crime, poverty, and lunacy caused by the excessive use of intoxicating liquors, have a right to the control of the number of places where such liquors are sold.

Before the expiration of the present Parliament we are told that Bills to assimilate the County and Borough Franchise, and to redistribute political power will be brought forward. I would give my best sup- port to well considered Bills on these subjects, and feel sure that they would be passed by a considerattlo majority of the present House of Commons. But they will require, too, the assent of the HOMO of Lords, and it is plain that the larger the majority is by which they are can led in the Lower House, the less likely is the House of Lords to resist the expressed mandate of the Nation. I appeal, therefore, to you, not to endanger the gift of the Franchise to your less fortu- nate neighbours, by returning as your Representative one who probably would vote against the full gift of the Franchise to the rural ratepayers, or, if he grudgingly assented to the equalised Franchise, would seek by a careful manipu7ation of boundaries, to make the gift ef as small effect as possible.

By the exerti,ns and self-sacrifice of the Viceroy and Chief Secretary, agrarian crime has diminished in Ire- land, whilst the ameliorating influence of the Land Court and of the At rears Bill is beginning to have effect. A mutinous conspiracy, such as has from time to time appeared in countries where society is disorgan- ised, has however been brought to light, and has shocked thcse most who had the greatest hopes of the effect of recent legislation. I would urge, however, here and elsewhere, that such crimes are not of the peaple, but imported among them, and that our policy must still be to act with patience. justice, and sym- pathy.

The beneficent rule. of Lord Ripon in India has re- sulted in such an equalisation of the Balt Duties, as to allow imported salt to compete on fair terms with the native product. I have no doubt but that, when the trade has adjusted itself, the full adoption of the prin- ciples of Free Trade intbis article will result in a large increase in our exports of salt, thus conferring'abenefit on the motives of India, as well as increasing the prosperity of our Cheshire salt trade.

I have lived among you now for over 30 years. You have had opportunities of knowing my public and my private life, and in asking you for your votes on this occasion as one who has hitherto tried to serve his fellow-men, I would in all humility, but with confi- dence, appeal to your knowledge of the past as the safest guarantee for my good conduct in the future.
I am, your obedient servant. GEORGE WILLIAM LATHAM.
Brad wall Hall, Sandbach, February 27th, 1883. .

- - - SIX LITTLE SISTERS. Six little sisters, so merry and gay— Hair of all colours, save snowy or grey ; Brownie and golden, golden and brown; Twisted and plaited. and hanging down. Cheeks pale or rosy, or colour of peach; Lips like ripe cherries have all, and have each; Byes brown as berries, coal-black, or as blue As the sky—a sure sign that their owner is true Six little sisters to stand on the floor; Six little sisters to file through the door; Six little sisters to laugh or to cry; Six little sisters to smile or to sigh; Six little sisters to dance in the light; Six little sisters to sleep through the night; Six little sisters, as merry as crickets— To tea: their white frocks in the thorns and the thickets. Six little sisters—a class without more— Trying to add to the length of their lore; Efii little sisters for multiplication; Six little sisters to do their dictation. Six little sisters for A. B, and C; Six little Asters for sewing at three. In summing, be sure they are ne'er in a fix, For they a&ays remember that six ones are six Six little sisters, so precious and dear! Close to perfection (won't reach it, I fear!) ; Six little sisters, all careless of care, Six little sisters, and not one to spare! Six little maidens—much better than boys ! Famed for their powers of making a noise. Six little sisters their "pieces" to strum; Six little sisters to sit on a thumb Six sweet little sisters; they come to you now With a smile and a frown, and a speech and a bow. Six dear little sisters—as good as red gold, Who yet may be better some day, we are told! Six little sisters, in best bibs and tuckers, Ribbons and frilligigs, flounces and puckers, Six little sisters, so coaxing and gay, To beg for a holiday once in a way! Well, they shall have it, then! Back in disgrace Pack all the lesson-books into their place. Down in the kitchen tease cook, till she bakes For the six little sisters six giant plum-cakes. This is their holiday—fun, falls, and knocks— Dan't shake your head, nurse, o'er rents in the frocks; Never mind scratches and tangleeome curls— They are six little sisters—and girls will be girls!

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- CULTURE, &c.

Mr. 5, Spencer, St. Ives, states that one of his young sows of the large white breed has lately dropped 18 Xolly-de- veloped pigs at her first litter, when under twelve months - old. One of his sows of the same strain of blood had 18 and 16 pigs at consecutive litters last year. INFLUENCE OF EARTHWORMS ON THE FERTILITY OF A Som.—The last work of the late Mr. Darwin left but little room for new matter under this head. Still, R. Hensen, after briefly summarising the facts already known, publishes a number of analyses of "worm earth," comparing it with ordinary soil, and showing that the composition of such earth is not much unlike that of the common leaf mould, so largely used by gardeners on account of its richness in humus. As is well known, the earthworm eats earth, pri- marily for the purpose of forming or excavating its burrow, and the soil in passing through the alimentary canal of the worm feeds directly on decayed vegetable matter. Worms bring about an even distribution of natural manurial matter in the soil; in the removal of leaves and other loose par- ticles !foal exposure to the wind to the shelter of the mouths of their burrows they lead up to a more rapid de- cay of organic matter. As a rule, they live in the upper soil, descending lower only in very cold weather. The tun- nels they make in the soil are of great value, not only in aiding the free growth of rootlets, but as containing air rich in carbonic acid gas, the solvent action of which on the mineral food of plants is of great importance. Such passages too, are of use in holding moisture, particularly. during frosty weather. LAwrrs.—lt would be impossible to state dogmatically at what intervals a lawn should be mown, as this must much depend upon the season, the state of the weather, and the rapidity with which the grass grows. It is, however, always desirable to begin mowing before the grass has attained undue length in the spring, and during the summer to cut it as frequently as possible; a week is the extreme period during which it should be left throughout the grass- growing months, and, to keep the lawn in really fine order, it should be mown much oftener. With the machine mower the labour of going over the lawn on which the grass is short is very slight, and the roller attached to the machine will then be generally sufficient to keep down worm and ant hills. In those cases where worms are so numerous as to become a nuisance, they may be dpstroyed by sprinkling the plot, through the rose of a watering-pot with water, into which, on the previous day, hot quick-lime has been thrown, in the proportion of six or eight pounds to the hogshead; it is, however, doubtful whether worms are not frequently as beneficial as hurtful by rendering the ground porous and admitting air to the roots of the grasses. Where such weeds as plantain, or ribbed grass, exist, they should be carefully rooted out, as they will destroy all the finer grasses near them. Moss, which results from poverty of the soil, is best destroyed by enriching it with top-dress- ings, such as guano, soot, fine compost lime, dm., applied early in the spring, and well brushed in. Treating the lawn in this manner, and using a collecting mower, is, in the opinion of some persons, preferable to the practice of scattering the grass; but the latter mode certainly affords nourishment to the grass.-r-Cassell's Household Guide. Goon BirrrEE AND GOOD Pnicns.—" I always find out what is the top price of the market, and then charge id. per lb. more—that's my way of doing business." He was a capital farm manager in charge of a glebe farm who was speaking, and he was talking about his butter. The top price has been is. 9d. a lb, and he had got is. 10d. last market day. "We always attend the market, my wife or I, and already we are taking in four and five dozen every week." There was a herd of twenty-five cows, getting good hay and meal and water; no cabbages or turnips or mangels were allowed. The stock included forty or fifty stores of various ages, and the farm was prospering, for there was plenty of cattle and sheep on it. "Of course I sell all I can to private houses, and if they complain of the price; I tell them it shall come down a id. next week, if they then want to get rid of me. Bless you, what is a id. a pound against good butter, or even 3d. or 4d. a pound if it is to be saved by buying that which is inferior. When owe I get a customer I can always keep him. He is not going to refuse my good butter because he can get cheaper in the next street. It is all made by my wife, who was brought up a townswoman, and never saw a pound of butter made in her life till she came to me." Don't your flatter yourself, my friend, that it needs anyone to be brought up to it to . succeed. All that it requires is but ordinary ability along with a resolution not to fail—nothing more than that! And whatever may be your prejudice against outsiders in agriculture, I could quote many another case besides the one given me by this bailiff in a midland county. There is no protection in agricultural competition except superior capability; and that comes we suspect not so much of breeding as of attention, carefulness, and resolution.—Agri- cultural Gazette. THE TURNIP FLY AND " FINGER-AND-TOE " IN TURNIPS. —Valuable and well-illustrated original articles upon these subjects—which will well repay perusal—are contained in the Annual Catalogue of Farm Seeds for 1883, issued by that enterprising firm of seed growers and manure manu- facturers, Messrs. Webb and Sons, Wordsley (Stourbridge), London, and Paris, who state in their address that they now annually employ nearly 12,000 acres for seed growing pur- poses. This catalogue is an enlarged edition and is an ex- cellent specimen of its kind; many high-class wood engrav- ings illustrate its pages, and several beautifully executed coloured plates of natural and other grasses are conspicuous, being novel features in a seedsman's list, and adding very much to its appearance. Permanent grass seeds are offered in mixtures specially arranged to suit the various geological formations, which are divided into 13 different classes or schedules; and Messrs. Webb also offer mixtures of per- manent grass seeds without rye-grass, agreeable to Mr. Faunce de Lanne's theory. Testimonials rrom landowners and tenant farmers in all parts of the kingdom •refer in the highest terms to Webb's grass seeds for all soils—one " cer- ' tificate of quality" sent by authority of his Grace the Duke of Marlborough, speaks very favourably of grass seeds for over 1,000 acres that Messrs. Webb supplied for this nobleman's estates last year. The seed-corn part of the catalogue is enlarg44 and contains many interesting parti- culars; and the varieties of swede, mangel, and turnip are described. Messrs. Webb give details of their special manures for all crops, and state that they have found it necessary to erect much larger manure works at Widnes, owing to the great increase in demand for these well-known fertilisers. Particulars of several hundreds of pounds given as prizes by Messrs. Webb and Sons at the leading agricul- tural shows during the ensuing season are stated, as well as various cultural instructions and a list of Champion and other prizes gained with the produce of their seeds in 1882 are also given.

Teacher (severely) : "John, why is it that boys' hands are always dirtier than girls' ?' John (hesitatingly) : "Please, sir, the girls washes the dishes." A regular physician, being sent for by a quack, expressed his surprise on being called in on an occasion apparently trifling. "Not so trifling, either," replied the quack; "for, to tell you the truth, I have by mistake taken some of my own pills." A fellow having kicked a newsboy for pestering him to buy in evening paper, the lad waited till another boy accosted the "gentleman," and then shouted in the hearing of all the bystanders: "It's no use to try him, Jim; he can't read." The most agreeable of all companions is a simple, frank person, without any pretension to an oppressive greatness; one who loves life and understands the use of it; is obliging alike at all hours; above all, of a golden temper, and stead- fast as an anchor. It is difficult for an honest man to make a living in some parts of London. A second-hand clothier in the East End was recently heard to moan—" \Then, Vhell Efery time I tell der truth I lose money, and efery times I lie I lose a customer. How can an honest man make a living ?"

"We frequently see it stated," says Mr. Oddfish, "that such and such men started from extreme poverty, coming into town in the first place without a farthing of money, and rising by their own exertions. When I first came I had to borrow money to get here, and I've been borrowing money ever since. It is a great thing at 60 to have estab- lished such a wonderful credit."

Cuyler. "And 'what age is it you are now, dear?" asked the camel just back from India of the tall daughter of his friend, Tomkinson Smith. "Well, that is what I can't quite make out," returned the girl, taking care to avoid her mother's eye, "for when I go anywhere with papa I am 16, but when I go out with mamma I am never more than 12 next birthday !" The colonel hastened to change the subject.

At a dinner party the little son of the host and hostess was allowed to come down to dessert. Having had what his mother considered a sufficiency of fruit, he was told he must not have any more, when, to the surprise of every one of the guests, he exclaimed, "If you don't give me some more, I'll tell !" A fresh supply was at once given him, and as soon as it was finished he repeated his threat, where- upon he was suddenly and swiftly removed from the room, but he had just time to convulse the company by exclaim- ing, "My new trousers are made out of ma's old bedroom curtains I"

--- MACAULAY'S HOME LIFE.—His sister, Lady Trevelyan, says that those who did not know him there "never knew him in his most brilliant, witty, and fertile vein." He was life and sunshine to young and old in the sombre house in Great Ormond-street, where the forlorn old father, like a blighted oak, lingered on in leafless decay, reading one long sermon to his family on Sunday afternoons, and another long sermon on Sunday evenings—" where Sunday walking for walking's sake was never allowed, and even going to a distant church was discouraged." Through this Puritanic gloom Macaulay shot like a sunbeam, and turned it into a fairy scene of innocent laughter and mirth. Against Idacaulay, the author, severe things, and just as severe, may be said; but as to his conduct in his own home—as a son, as a brother, and an uncle—it is only the barest justice to say that he appears to have touched the furthest verge of human virtue, sweetness, and generosity. His thinking was often, if not generally, pitched in what we must call a low key, but his action might put the very saints to shame. He reversed a practice too common among men of genius, who are often careful to display all their shining and attractive qualities to the outside world, and beep for home consump- tion their meanness, selfishness, and ill-temper. Macaulay struck no herotc attitude of benevolence, magnanimity, and aspiration before the world—rather the opposite; but in the circle of his home affections he practised those virtues without letting his right hand know what was done by his loft.

WOMEN AS SANITARIANS.—I am bold to intimate that it lumld be exceedingly wise also to let women become eligible for seats on local sanitary boards; for women are by nature sanitarians ; they see the lights of health and the shads TS of disease mach more acutely and keenly than men do. They are quick at suggesting sound and whole- some reforms; they know infinitely more about the domes- tic life and the home than men know; when they are well Informed and interested they are allies of the first order; while, when they are not informed and are not interested in reforms, they are opponents which no man and no board can withstand. I take it, indeed, as impossible to make the slightest further permanent advance in sanitation unless the women of the country move with us men in the effort. Again, I take it as certain that if the women were to move with us heartily and intelligently in sanitation we men would very soon have very little to do. For things are what they spring from. The great rivers are rivulets, the oeeans are rivers; and if from those millions of living rivulets which we call homes, over which the woman rules by right as well as. by custom, we could see health, and nothing but health, issue forth; the rivers of health were made, the oceans were made, and the great earth were laved by the seas of healthy life. But if we would get the mmds of our women imbued with the importance of the work for health we have in hand, we must let them see the bearings of that work in its outer as well as its inner cha- racter. We must let them learn by practice the 'truth that the necessity for rule and governance outside the home originates from imperfect rule and governance inside the home. We must, in a word, let them share with men in the knowledge of public responsibilities.—Dr. B. W. _Richardson, in " Longinan's May azine." TEE CANARY ISLANDS.—One very interesting fact in reference to the Berber people is that the aboriginal but now extinct inhabitants of the Canary Islands owed their origin to this race. These lovely islands—the "fortunate isles" of the early Roman poets, the "Hesperides," or islands of the blest," of many a songwriter since' where tte souls of the departed dead rested—a region lying beyond ie then limitless sea, where the horizon was lit up by the iya of the setting sun—seem to have been peopled in com, pirefively recent times; for when Juba 11., the African King of Iffutritania, explored them—as narrated by Pliny —there seemed to have been few inhabitants on the islands. In modern times they were first explored between the years 1326 and 1334. Theirhistory is the history of any country on which the Spanish race ever set foot. Slaves were con- tioually taken on different expeditions made to them by We people, and in one of them the "King and Queen of Lausarote " and seventy of the inhabitants were captured and earned into slavery. In the year 1402 Messire Jean de Bethenceurt, a Norman knight, subdued the islands, in spite of the gallant resistance of the inhabitants, who were called Gnanchee." At that time there were about 9,000 people in Canaria. Grande, and 5,000 on Tenerife. The natives were said to have been tall, but of simple habits and few arts, knew nothing of metals, and ploughed the land with the ho-rns of bullocks. They believed in a future state, and worshipped a supreme being called Achoron Achaman.,, They also believed in a malignant being, " Yruena," and that the abode of the wicked was in a cavern on the side of Tevde. Marriage and various other moral and social insti- tutions were established i amongst them. They embalmed the dead, and laid the bodies n caverns or catacombs in the' sides of mountains where they have been found since the depopulation of the islands. These mummies were placed erect, with their feet against the sides of the cave; the chiefs, with a staff in their hands, and a vessel of milk by their sides. The mummies were prepared by saturating the boiy with a kind of turpentine, and then drying it before a slow fire or in the sun. In the tombs were laid aromatic plants, and the corpses were decorated with laces, on which were hung little dishes of baked earth, and the whole body wrapped in bandages of goatskin. The body was filled with .a kind of grain resembling rice. It was not, however, until 1496 that the Camarians were thoroughly subdued, and in a few years the remnant, after being forced to be baptised, were either exterminated or sold into slavery. It is a pretty tale of piracy, bigotry, sanctity, and murder that llessire de Bethenoourt has to. tell us—a tale, unfortunately, not Mans in those (lays, nor for several centuries since.—Front The Petplies of Me Worl4.

In all evils which admit a remedy impatience should be avoided, because it wastes that time and attention in com- plaints which, if properly applied, would remove the cause. Gravity does not indicate wisdom any more than silence, nor is a turn for conversation of a cheerful, instructive character the distinctive mark of fools, whatever stupid dulness may hint on the subject. There is nothing so certain to insure success in life—real success—as thorough honesty of character, and a habitual abhorrence on principle of all petty meanness, artfulness, disguises, and the many social hypocracies of the age. A nurse was telling about a man' that had become so terribly worn out by dissipation that he could not keep any food on his stomach, when one of her listeners asked, "What does he live on, then ?" "On his relations, ma'am," answered the nurse. LEGAL DELIGHTS.—The man who has never been a de- fendant in an action at law has never tasted one of the chief pleasures of existence. He is probably served with a writ, and his servants, and perhaps his wife, begin to suspect that he is connected in some mysterious way with the Dynamite Brotherhood. He goes to a solicitor, and, after several days of patient teaching, he will have taught that solicitor some- thing about his case. In due time the solicitor will take the same trouble, second-hand, to teach a barrister ; after which the barrister—if the case goes into court—will take the trouble, third-hand, if he is not called into another court, to teach the Judge; and the Judge, fourth-hand, will take the trouble to teach the jury. The man now called a client will be asked in writing the most insulting ques- tions, called "interrogatories," and these he will be ex- pected to answer without losing his temper. Various legal messengers will now wait upon him at various hours of the day to swear various affidavits. He will be asked to step out and find a commissioner empowered to take oaths, and after trying two ground floors and three first floors, will discover one of these privileged persons in an airy garret. He will now learn the meaning and beauty of the word venue. He may be sued in Yokelshire, or he may be sued in Clogshire. In the latter case he will be marched down to Mudchester with his solicitor and a small party of wit- nesses—the majority of whom will never be wanted. He will be fed with reports that he is Number Four on the list, and may come on at any moment. After waiting a week he will find that Mudchester has more cases than it can try, and he is marched off with his party to the neighbouring town of Livelypool. Here he is comforted with the as- surance that he will "come on" at the opening of the as- sizes, and, in consequence, he has only to wait four days for his long-expected trial. His case is sure to be one that can only be properly judged without favour or prejudice by a London jury; but, if the venue is laid in Clogshire, he must be tried by the natives. He finds his solicitor and barrister sitting in cramped pews, with huge bundles of paper before them the size of hotel pillows. These papers seem to make them very unhappy; but still' they cling to them. Being about the longest documents in existence: they are cOled "briefs," and no not appear necessary 0 any person who can write the history of England on a shirt- cuff. The barristers get tired of these unwieldly documents before the trial is half over, and are thankful to any one— even to the "client"—who will give them information that can be put upon a railway ticket. The case ivill.probablr be ably argued on both sides, without temper or bad taste— for the Northern Circuit is served by leading lawyers and Judges—but the jury will doubtless take their own view in spite of evidence and ruling. The client-will have the pleasure of obtaining a new trial in London, if he likes to apply for jt, and if not, he will have learnt something for his money.—Punch.

The Italian Government has entrusted the restoration of the Basilica of San Paolo at Rome to the architect Valen- tino Grazioli. The restoration was begun by Count IT es- pignani, the late Papal architect. Manganese bronze is growing rapidly in favour as a material for screw propeller blades. It is very strong, and its durability far exceeds that of steel, the life of which in a propeller averages about three years. A propeller made of bronze will, however, last as long as the vessel, and after- wards be of considerable money value. M. Mauser has succeeded in devising an arrangement by which a hundred telephones may be spoken through by one person; that is, one person may speak to a hundred audi- tors in different places at the- same time. The economic advantages of this innovation will probably appear in due time. The result has been obtained by augmenting the tension of the current. _

The foundations of a Roman villa have been found in the village of Furschweiler, near St. Wendel. It has been built of rubble and very firm lime mortar. An altar in the Atrium is in good preservation, and from the bones of deer -found near it seems to have been dedicated to Diana. Earthen and iron vessels were found near. From the remains of charred beams and woodwork it is concluded that. the villa was destroyed by fire. M. Brown-Sequard communieated to the Academy of Sciences at its last sitting a notice on the phenomenon which he has named "inhibition." This term he applies when a lesion at a point of the nervous system causes the sudden suspension of some function or activity of nerve force. If, for instance, the nervous system be injured at some essential but relatively remote point, the suspension of respiration calorificatioat, circulation, etc., may follow. The Atheneum states that Mr. Millar, of the Dundee Advertiser, has finished his" History of ROI) Roy." He has made use in it of many of the documents and letters in the collections of the Duke of Argyll, the Duke of Montrose, the Duke of Athole and Sir-Robert Menzies. Many mythical stories which have long been in circulation regarding Rob Roy have been discarded, and the incidents of his career are for the first time placed in proper chronological order. REMOVING SCALE.—A correspondent of the American Manufactvprer writes :—" As a sort -of 'shop kink' I give a curious experiment tried on an engine water supply pipe that had become choked up with lime incrustation. After hammering it for an hour or two, and kindling a fire all over it, without any result, one end was plugged up, and about a pint of refined coal oil was poured in the other end—all it would hold—leaving it to stand all night. The next morn- ing the entire mass slid out a solid lime core. Before trying this we thought of throwing the pipe away as useless, and getting a new one." M. Deherain, reporting on experiments on plants at the Electric Exhibition at the Palais d'lndustrie in 1881, sums up his conclusions thus :-1. The electric arc light emits radiations which are injurious to vegetation. 2. Most of these radiations are arrested by colourless glass. 3. The electric light emits radiations powerful enough to maintain mature plants in vegetation for two months and a half.. 4. The beneficial radiations are not sufficiently powerful to cause the growth of germinating seeds, or to allow of the maturation of fruit in older plants. IMPORTANT BIBLICAL DISCOVERY IN EGYPT.—Mr. Regi- nald Stuart Poole, hon. secretary Egypt Exploration Fund, writes to the editor of the Daily Telegraph:—M. Neville writes from Tell-el-Maschuto to announce that the excava- tions undertaken by him on that site for the Egypt Ex- ploration Fund have already yielded a result of the first his- torical and geographical importance. This site—Tell-el- Maschuta—rougly midway between Ismailia and Tell-el- Kebir, is proved by an inscription dug up by M. Neville to be at once the Pithom and the Succoth of the Bible. Pithom was the sacred name descriptive of the Temple, and Succoth (Tuku) the civil appellation. We read of Pithom as one of the cities built, by the Israelites during the op- pression (Exodus, i.' 11), and Succoth Was their first station in the march of the Exodus (Exodus, xii. 37, xiii. 30.) The discovery not only places Pithom-Succoth in the map, but in doing so gives us at last a fixed point in the route of the Israelites out of Egypt. MANUFACruIiES IN THE UNITED STATES.—Statistics just published enable us to gain some idea of the progress which has been made during the last 30 years in the domes- tic manufactures of the United States. According to the census of 1850, the total value of these manufactures, in- cluding fisheries and the products of the mines was $1,019,106,616. Twenty years later—that is, in 187 d—the total value of the manufactured products throughout all the United States, gas being excepted, had risen to $4,232,325,442. In 1880 the value as returned by the Census Bulletin was no less than $5,360,667,706. In 30 years the manufactures had thus increased fivefold, and during the last ten years alone the increase in the value of the manufactured products had reached the very large sem of $1,137,342,264, or more than £27,000,000. In the pro- duction of the manufactures there were engaged 2,207,197 men and 581,753 women or 2,733,950 persons in all. It is calculated that each of these maintained on an average two-and-a-half other individuals, making the whole nrirn- ber of persons suppported by manufactures in the United States 9,586,325, or almost one-fifth of the entire popula- tion. This was exclusive of the number engaged in the _ _ _ _ _

production of many of the raw materials and- a food for the manufacturers; the distribution of their products, such as merchants, clerks, draymen, mariners, the employes of railroads, expresses, and steamboats; of capitalists, various artistic and professional classes, as well as carpenters, bricklayers, painters, and the members of other mechanical trades not classed as manufacturers. Altogether, one-third of the whole population may be said to be dependent upon the manufacturing industry. WHAT IS ASBESTOS ?—This word is now 80 frequently used in the industrial arts in paper-making, !cc., yet so little is known concerning the mysterious substance itself, which is incombustible—that the following particulars may be of interest. Asbestos, a Greek work which means inconsumable, is the name given to a variety of hornblende. The coarser grades are known as asbestos, and the finer, fibrous, more silky variety, as amianthus. The chemical composition of asbestine rocks is chiefly silicia, magnesia alumina, and fer- rous oxide. Amianthus, the most beautiful form of asbes- tos, is found in the Pyrenees, in Alps of Dauphiny, Mount St. Gothard, and in Sweden; but the finest specimens come from Travenbaise in Saxony, and from Corsica. It is in long white flexible fibres, as fine sometimes as the finest silk. Bergkork (mountain cork) and Bergholz (mountain wood) are coarser varieties, so called from their resemblance to cork and wood. Mountain cork is so light that it will float on water. Mountain leather is a variety possessing the same general character as mountain wood, but occurring in thin flexible sheets resembling leather. Properties of asbes- tos :—Native asbestos is found in thin, irregular veins, often requiring heavy blasting and hard work to extract. In the Alps alone there are over 100 distinct varieties. In a single thread asbestos is fusible before the blow-pipe; but in the mass it is practically infusible. Its infusibility depends on the percentage of iron in its composition. Those varieties which contain the smallest amount of iron are capable of .standing the highest heat without fusing or crumbling. It has not been mail within the last 50 years that the indus-
trial worth of asbestos has been fully recognised. The

ancients spun it into a fabric which was used a; a shroud or winding sheet, to prevent the ashes of the deceased mixing with those of the funeral pyre. It was also made by them into tablecloths and napkins, which were cleansed by throw- ing into the fire. The asbestine fibres were sometimes spun with flax, and the flax afterwards destroyed, leaving only the asbestos fibre. In those countries in which it is native the peasants have for centuries back used it for lamp wicks, . .

Asbestos is now extensively used in the manufacture of fire-proof roofing, as a packing for safe doors, as steam pack- ing for piston and pumping rods, stuffing boxes, mill boards, steam joints and man-hole plates, and as so-called "felting" to cover steam pipes and boilers. It is said that, used as a boiler covering, it saves 25 per cent, of heat that would otherwise be lost through radiation. As packing for piston rods it is excellent. The difficulty which was formerly met with—liability to crumble—has now been overcome by making the fibres into twisted or plaited rope. Wearing to a small surface, it needs much less lubrication than hemp or wool. It is also used for fire screens, as a backing for fire- places, to support porcelain ware while being burned in the furnace, and when combined with resin as electrical insula- lators. In the utilisation of hydro-carbon for fuel it pro- mises to take an important place. In this conneation k is used as a fuel-bed, and the hydro-carbons are burned thereon. It enters into many other manufactures more or less extensively, and promises to become of greater value every year.

TISH MIDLAND RAILWAY SHRYANTS AND THEIR WAGES. —An important agitation is going on amongst the servants of the Midland Railway all over the system from Carlisle to Bristol for the advance of their wages. Four years ago the passenger and goods guards and the porter e had their wages reduced 11. per week, in consequence of the depression in trade The reduction having been in force four years, and the receipts hem traffic and the dividend having in- creased, the men consider that it is now time that the is. skould be granted. Memorials from time to time have been presented to the directors of the company by the passenger guards without effect, and now the movement has extended to all classes of servants who suffered a reduction. Meetings are being held and petitions signed all over the system, urgently requesting that wages be restored to the old scale. A movement is also in progress with a view of getting over- time, or a relief fram Sunday duty, and establishing six days to the working week— all beyond that to be reckoned as overtime. The employe are hopeful that, considering the distinct promise made by the late Mr. Ellis, the directors will favourably consider the grievances complained of. IRON TRADIS STATISTICS.—Mr. J. S. Jeans, the secretary of the British Iron Trade Association, has compiled some interesting information regarding the past year, which is being issued to members of the association in advance of the annual statistical report. The returns show that enormous progress is being m ide in steel manufacture. The total productien of Bessemer steel ingots in the United Kingdom is stated at 1,673,649 tons, an increase of 231,930 tons on the production of the previous year. Seventy-four per cent. of the ingots made were manufactured into Bessemer steel rails, against 70 per cent. in 1881 and 1880, the production of rails being 1,235,785 tons, an increase of 212,045 tons on that of 1881. The largest quantities of ingots were turned out in South Walee and Sheffield. The number of Besse- mer converters at work during the year was 80, two less than in 1851, the average output per converter having in- creased from 17,582 tons to 20,920 tons. In 1879 the average yield per converter was only 12,641 tons. Tile best result obtained during 1882 was a make of 78,202, with two con- verters. The make of "open-hearth steel " was 436,000 tone, against 338,000 tons in 1881. Scotland is the chief seat of this industry, the production of the Scotch open- hearth works hiving been more than doubled during 1882 as campared with th et of the previous year. On Jannaiy 1, 1833, there were 1,082 487 tons of steel, iron, and wooden shipping in process of construction, or about to be built, in the United Kingdom, 182,116 tons lees than on January 1, 1882.

DOGS.—CARE IN WET WEATHER.—.Wet 'Weather is very bad for all kinds of dogs, at least for such as run out of doors, as it often lays the seeds of rheumatism and many other diseases, and consequently measures should be taken to prevent the mischief, so far as that is possible. Dogs that have been running with a carriage, or even knocking about without any such good reason generally come home wet, dirty, and bedraggled. This, in long coated dogs espe- cially, is very dangerous indeed, and the dirt ought to be washed off the legs and stomach, and the whole body well rubbed with a coarse towel, the friction from which, in addition to the mere drying, will be highly beneficial. In large kennels or with sporting dogs it is well to rub the body with some pot liquor, which is simply water in which mutton fat or tallow has been melted. Nothing can be more efficacious than this simple application, as the oil which reaches the skin not only prevents any chill or cold from the past, but will prepare the dog to resist cold the following day. It is well known that swimmers often anoint their bodies with oil to protect them from the numbing effect of the water, and thus prevent the exhaus- tion which follows cold. lind also iu the Franco-German War the soldiers in the German army, during that terrible winter, used flannel bandages which had been saturated with tallow, instead of stockings. After a dog has been cleaned in this way it should be allowed a good bed of straw, and probably will rub itself entirely dry in this. Dogs kept out of doors in kennels should have good bedding, and, as they have to stand all kinds of weather, it is a good plan every few days to rub some of the pot liquor named all over them. The cost will be very small, and when we take into consideration the prevention of suffering on the part of the animal, this will not be regarded at all by any one with the least instincts of humanity. And as to the trouble, if it is worth keeping a dog at all it is worth keeping it in a proper manner. Food should, of course, be good, and •a warm dish of broth, either by itself or with dog biscuits soaked in it, will be highly relished, and not only so, but probably prevent disease through cold. • It has been said by some one that cold first attacks the man who has an empty stomach, and this is equally as true in the case of dogs. PREPARING THE As:WAßß:M.—Having made the aquarium, the next thing is to prepare the bed of the pond. For this first obtain some fine gravel or sand, cleanse it thoroughly, which is best done by running clean water through it, until this comes out as it goes in. Then lay it on the bottom of the tank to the thickness of an inch at least, over which put small pebbles in different places. If rock work or miniature caverns are desired, pile up small blocks of granite, fastening them together with the best Portland cement, which is the best for this purpose, as other cements I are liable to taint the water, and thus injure the fish. Even 1 with the kind named it should be allowed to remain in the water for a week, so that if there are any soluble matters in ' it they may pass away. When the sand, gravel, and rockery , have been put in let the cement get firm, then add water, which can be allowed to remain over night, and emptied off next morning. This must be repeated, emptying and re- filling until the water is perfectly clear, and not until then should any plants be introduced into it. As we mentioned in one of our previous notes, thepresence of vegetable growth ' in the aquarium is necessary to maintenance of life in the finny inmates; and the plants which are thus grown add greatly to the appearance and to the interest of the pursuit. Almost as much pleasure can be derived in noting the de- velopments and different characteristics of the various plants, as in watching the fish themselves. Many plants can be ob- tained, some of which are rarer than others; but it will be better to consult some one who understands the same as to 1 the kinds to be selected, and very often those who sell the aquariums are in a position to supply the other requisites , also. The best method of planting the weeds ia to tie each I of them to a pebble, and sink them below the surface of the , shingle. A little care in doing this will greatly help the , effect, the ehorter to be at the front and the longer behind. i After all the plants are arranged a little duckweed may be thrown in, as this floats upon the surface, and is a harbour for minute insects, which serve as dainty morsels for the fish. Before any fish are introduced, the plants should be given time to establish themselves, which will be about a fortnight. Should by this time a green film have been found to spread itself over the surface of the glass, this must be taken as a sign, either that too much light has been given, or too many plants have been introduced, in proportion to the quantity of water. lo.—ln order to help readers of The Examiner over any difficulties they may meet with, the writer of the above notes will be pleased to answer any questions rela, ing to Dogs. Pigeons. Cage Birds, Rabbits, and Pets. their management or diseases, that may be put to him. These must be concise, yet contain all impor ant particulars, and be addressed to " Emma-er Office, Warrington, and contain the name and address t of the lorrespcndents. not neeeesarily for publication, but as a f ;uarantee of so xl faith.

div.head: CHESHIRE MURDERS.
div.p: THE CHESHIRE MURDERS.

Patrick Carey, alias Jack White, who is suspected of having, on the 19th inst., brutally murdered Thos. Earlam, a lodging-house keeper at Smallwood. near Congleton, and Earlarn's housekeeper, Mary Moran, was apprehended on Saturday at a low lodging-house, off Charter-street, Man- chester, by Detective-Sergeant Jackson and Detective Fox, of the Manchester Detective Department. He was at once conveyed to the Town Hall, and information of the capture sent to the Cheshire police, and they in the course of the day sent over several persons who fully identified the pri- soner as being the man wanted. On Monday be was taken before the justices at the City Police Court charged with the murder. Only formal evidence was given as to the man's identity, and he was handed over to the custody of an officer of the Cheshire Constabulary. ' At the Sandbach Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. G. W. Latham, Patrick Carey, alias John White, was charged with the wilful murder of Thomas Earlam and Mary Moran, on the 9th inst., at Smallwood, near Sandbach. A large crowd assembled outside the court, but owing to the limited accommodation but few persons were able to gain admit- tance to the inquiry,—Police-Superintendent John Hindley, of Middlewich, was the drat witness called. He said: On Friday, the 9th February, I went to the house at Smallwood occupted'by Thomas Earlam and Mary Moran. I saw the body of Thomas Earlam, and there were signs of blows on the head. I also saw the woman Mary Moran on the follow- ing Monday. She was not then dead, but wounded badly in the head and unconscious. On the 19th inst. I saw her dead body.—Wm. Booth, police-constable at Smallwood, said: I remember Friday, the 9th February. About 12-50 p.m. on that day I met the prisoner near the house formerly occu- pied by Earlam and Moran. He was on the Congleton-road, land perhaps half a mile away from the house. lie had with him a bundle made up in a coloured handkerchief.—Patrick Shannon repeated the evidence he gave at the Manchester City Police Court, on Monday. Until the Monday before the murder he had lodged with the prisoner at Earlam's house. On the day of the murder witness was not there.— The prisoner was asked if he had any questions to put to the witnesses, and in reply he merely shook his head. He was then remanded for a week. In the course of the after- noon he was removed to Knutsford gaol.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND. THE MURDER CONSPIRACY. LETTER FROM BRENNAN.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND. THE MURDER CONSPIRACY. LETTER FROM BRENNAN.

There appears in the Freeman's Journal of Tuesday a letter dated "London, 23rd February," and signed "Thomas Brennan," in which the writer says :—" In your issue of the 20th instant there appeared a Renter's telegram to the effect that the British Government had made no request to the State Department at Washington for my extradition, thereby implying that I had fled to America, and that I was liable to arrest even in that country on some very serious charge. While I do no not now feel called upon either to admit or deny the accurracy of the statement that I at one time belonged to what has been referred to during the Kilmainham investiga- tion as the Irish Republican Brotherhood, I must emphati- cally deny that it is in the power of the English Government to advance any charge against me that would come within the meaning of the International Law of Extradition. If they want me on such a charge I will save them the trouble of applying to the American Government." _

div.head: DEMAND FOR SHERIDAN'S EXTRADITION.
div.p: DEMAND FOR SHERIDAN'S EXTRADITION.

The British Government has telegraphed to its represen- tative in America to demand the extradition of P. J. Sheridan, who has been so promineetly mentioned in con- nection with the Dublin murder conspiracy. The necessary ti,cuments, duly authenticated, were forwarded by mail on Tuesday to New York, and will be laid before the American judicial authorities in due course. The extradition of Sheridan is demanded under the extradition clause of the Ashhurnham Treaty, which provides "that Great Britain and the United States shall deliver up to each other all per- sons charged with the crime of murder or assault to commit murder, provided that this shall only be done upon such evidence of criminality as according to the laws of the place where the fugitive or person so charged shall be found would justify his apprehensibn and commit- ment for trial, if the ct ime or offence had there been com- mitted, and the respective judges of the respective Govern— ments shall have power, jurisdiction, and authority, upon complaint made upon oath, to issue a warrant for the appre- hension of the fugitive or person so charged, that he may be brought before such judges or other magistrates respec- tively to the end that the evidence of criminality may be heard and considered, and if upon such hearing the evidence of criminality be heard and considered proved, it shall be the duty of the examining judge or magistrate to certify the same to the proper executive authority, that a warrant may issue for the surrender of such fugitive." This extra- dition would be based upon the presumption of the British law that an accessory to murder is equally guilty with the priacipal. ANOTHER INQUIRY AT DUBLIN CASTLE.

An inquiry was commenced at Dublin Castle on Saturday which, according to report, has for its object the connecting; of the numerous agrarian murders in Ireland with the assas- sination conspiracy recently brought to light. The police are said to be of opinion that they have got to the root of the matter, and to be sanguine that within a very short time the murderers of Mrs. Smythe, Mr. llerbert, and Mr. Blake and his servant will be in custody. LE ITER FROM GEN. MACADARAS, THE SUP-

div.head: POSED "No. 1."
div.p: POSED "No. 1."

General Macadaras has telegraphed as follows to the Chief Secretary for Ireland :—" I am ready and willing to submit to the most rigid scrutiny of my actions, and have made this fact known to Lord Lyons." The Times says : Mr. Macadaras writes to us, under date Paris, February 21, 1833, to express his disgust and mortification at a report published concerning him in an evening paper. "I request," he says, " that you will in courtesy publish this my protest against being made the target for unscrupulous and infamous libel, and I beg to inform you that I have instructed my solicitors to take immediate action in the matter. I would not even condescend to refute what must be well known to my numerous friends and acquaintances as an infamous libel. I request that you will do me the favour of pub- lishing this letter to the public." ARREST OF MR. FRANK BYRNE.

Mr. Frank Byrne was arrested in Paris on Tuesday and taken to the Prefecture of Police, is still confined there, and is allowed to receive no visits. On being questioned by the Public Prosecutor, Mr. Byrne repeated the reply that he had already given to the Prefect of Police. He admitted that his name was Byrne, but stated that he was secretary to the English Land and Labour League, and not cf the Irish Land League. Mr. Byrne added that he was not guilty of assassination, and declined subsequently to answer any further questions. Nothing has yet been decided in regard to his extradition, which forms the subject of careful con- sideration. The final decision in the matter will only be taken by the Council of Ministers. ANOTHER DISCOVERY IN DUBLLN. On Tuesday evening, a tire broke out in a hay store in Pill-lane, Dublin, which is rented by an iror.monger named Luke Doyle. The fire was speedily extinguished on the arrival of the brigade, but in the course of a subsequent ex- amination of the premises by the police a discovery was. made to which considerable importance is attached. Under the staircase were discovered a large quantity of revolver cartridges, and a pocket book containing a number of American greenbacks, and some documents of, it is stated, an important character. Both the ammunition and the pocket book and the contents were at once taken possession of by the police. It may be remembered that Robert Far- rell, the informer, stated that he had been in the employ- ment of Mr. Doyle, of Pill-lane. Mr. Doyle denies he knows anything about the articles which were found, and has not been arrested, but the police are actively enquiring into the matter.
There is reason to believe that Judge Lawson, who is at present in Italy, will shortly resume his judicial duties.

Mr. Timothy Harrington was, on Saturday, elected, with- out opposition, to represent the county of Westmeath, in the room of Mr. 11. J. Gill, resigned. Mr. Harrington is now in prison at Mallingar. Mr. P. J. Sheridan has declared, in an interview with a representative of the press, that he never met the informer Carey. He also denied all complicity in the Phoenix Park murders. At a meeting of rafepayers held at Galway, the other even- ing, it was resolved to request Mr. John orrell Lever, the member for the borough, to resign his seat. A requisition to that effect was drawn up and signed by nearly six hundred electors,

There comes from Ballydehob, county Cork, a story of the finding in the Post.office there a parcel addressed to Earl Spencer containing six minces of dr)mite and a fuse. The postmaster is stated to have " indiocreeVi burned the address label."

Colonel King-Harman (Conservative Home Ruler) has been elected for county Dublin by a majority of upwards of a thousand votes over the Nationalist candidate, Mr. M'Mahon. Only 13 votes were recorded for Mr. Guinness, I the independent Conservative. At the contest in March, 1874, the late Colonel Taylor (Conservative) polled 331 votes I fewer than Colonel King-Harman received this time, and Mr. Parnell, his opponent, nearly 200 fewer than Mr. M'Mahon. It will thus be seen that there was on Tuesday a very heavy vote. Four-fifths of the electors were polled. The Conser- vative candidate was also successful at Portarllngton. He received 70 votes against the Nationalist candidate's 57. THE IRISH PARTY AND THE LAND ACT.—The bill which has been introduced 13y the Irish party for the amendment. of the Land Act proposes some important changes in the existing law. It is provided that amongst other alterations the judicial rent shall date from the rent day next succeeding the date of a tenant's application to the court; that proceedings to enforce payment of rent shall be stayed pending the fixture of a fair rent; and that no rent shall be made payable on a tenant's improvement. These and several minor changes in the Land Act were, it will be remembered, fully discussed when the measure was passing through the House of Commons, and were all resisted y the Government. ATTEMPT TO MURDER A BAILIFF OF LORD ARDILA UN'S. —A desperate attempt has been made to murder another of I Lord Ardilaun's bailiffs, within a short distance of the mur- der of the two Huddys. It appears that on Sunday the bailif, Flynn, in charge of a farm of Lord Ardilaum's, was spending the day at the village of Uornamona. He left there about four o'clock and proceeded on his way home. When a short distance from Cornamona he was joined on the road by a man whom Flynn says he does not know. They walked along the road until they arrived at a turn which interrupted the view of the village of Cornamona, when a man suddenly jumped over the wall and made a desperate attempt to murder Flynn. Both men joined in the attempt, and left Flynn when it was supposed he was dead. No arrests have been made. Flynn is not expected to recover.

ATTACK ON THE MAAMTRASNA WITNESSES —A serious -affray occurred on Sunday evening between the Maamtrasna Crown witnesses and a party of men who were drinking in Boyle's public-hourse at Churchfield. The three Joy ces, the principal witnesses in the murder case, accompanied by five men of the Irish Constabulary to protect them, went into the house for refreshment. A number of men were there drinking, and a quarrel ensued. The police, la endeavour- ing tq protect the Joyces, were overpowered and deprived of their sidearms, which were freely used on the Joyces. Antony Joyce was badly wounded, and the others received sword thrusts. Both parties were severely beaten. Inlsrt M.P.'s Is GAOL—The Freeman's Journal says: —At preeent the Government have the member for West- meath irt a convict's dress, picking oakum in Mullingar Gaol; they have the member for Wexford under watch and ward, locked up in Richmond Prison; and Mr. O'Kelly is under suspension for a week. The Freeman proceeds to give details of tke treatment of Mr. Harrington, the hon. member for Westmeath, now a prisoner in Mullingar Gaol, and declares that it is a shame to attempt by physical indignities, to inflict a moral strain upon men in Mullingar Gaol. It says there are no sanitary conveniences. The prisoners are locked up 22 ' hours out of 24. A tin vessel is placed in each man's cell, and ter the wants of nature he must use this and keep it in his cell all night. The system in Mullingar Gaol is that each man when liberated in the morning shall parade in the yard with his tin bucket and its contents. The men are then marched across the yard, past the governor's house, and to the banks of a running stream, which they are com- pelled to pollute with the contents of their slop buckets, and are then marched back with these utensils again past the I governor's house. This was Mr. Harrington's task on the morning of his election as member of Parliament. The Freeman maintains that not even the pickpocket should be subjected to such sanitary conditions, which are calculated to breed pestilence. I -

The foot and mouth disease has this week been rapidly spreading in Derbyshire, fresh outbreaks being reported in 11 places. FATAL POISONING CASH IN A WORKIIOUSE.—i month ago a domestic servant, a girl named Ada Hamraond, died at the Sheffield workhouse under circuinstauces that led to the supposition that she had been poisoned. At the ad- journed inquest, on Wednesday, the report of an analyst who had analysed the contents of the stomach was read. Tbig showed that death was caused by an irritant poison, probably rue or savin. There was no evidence to show by whom it was administered, and an open verdict was re- turned. The girl, who was caly sixteen years of age, bad recently jilted her lover.

Mr. Tunstall said he appeared as an overseer. Mr. Ridgway objected to Mr. Tunstall appearing as an overseer, or in any other capacity. Mr. Sutton : Mr. Tunstall is not appearing as an I, overseer, but as a person who claims to be heard as an ' overseer. Mr. Ridgway : To protect my rights I object to that. Mr. Tunstall then quoted from 4 and 5 William IV., cap. 7, sec. 109, the following :—" The word 4 overseer' shall be construed to mean and include overseers of the poor, churchwardens, se far as they are authorised or required by law to act in the management or relief of the poor, or in the collection or distribution of the poor rate, assistant overseer, or any other subordinate officer, whether paid or unpaid, in any parish or union, who shall be employed therein, in carrying this Act or the laws for the relief of the poor, into execution. The word 'officer ' shall be construed to ex- tend to any clergyman schoolmaster, person duly licensed to practice as a medical man, vestry clerk, treasurer, collector, assistant overseer, governor, master or mistress of a workhouse, or any other person who shall be employed in any parish or union in carrying this Act, or the laws for the relief of the poor into execution, and whether perform- ing one or more of the above-mentioned functions." Mr. Sutton, however, advised Mr. Tunstall not to speak, and Mr. Ridgway went on to say that it appeared—and he believed there was no dispute as to the facts—that a number of these claims, some 60 or so, were delivered to Mr. John Laverock Tunstall, who was, as he was informed, one of the clerks in the assistant overseer's office, on the 31st January' in the present year. But these claims, to which he objected, were not delivered to Mr. Tunstall at the overseers' office or at the house of any overseer, but were delivered to him in his own private residence, 21, Arpley-street, in War rington. He was further informed—and he believed there was DO dispute as to this portion of the case—that Mr. Tun- stall did not take these notices to any one of the overseers or the office of the overseers until the morning of the Ist February. He believed the rest of the notices were served upon Mr. Tunstall likewise, not at his private house but at his private office in Sankey-street. Thus arose the question at issue between them—whether these notices had been duly served, and whether Mr. Tunstall was a person or e. sub- ordinate officer who came within the meaning of the de- finition of the word" overseer" in section 109,4 and 5, Wm. covered from the Governor of Jamaica for the detention of I the Florence. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TnunspAy. NEW WRITS AND NEW MEMBER—New writs were issued for Wycombe and Mid-Cheshire, and Colonel E. R. King- Harman took the oaths and his seat for county Dublin. TRH .BUDGET.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer pro- mised to fix a day after Easter upon which he would make his financial statement. THE INDIAN CONTINGENT.—Mr. ONSLOW endefrvoured to obtain explanations as to the negotiations with the Government of India respecting the employment of the Indian contingent, but Lord lIARTINGTON replied that he had promised papers when there was very little hope of any substantial agreement being come to between the twa Govern- ments. Since then, however, Her Majesty's Government had made a proposal to the GOvernment of India which had been accepted, and there would be some disadvantage to India from the publication of the correspondence between the two departments, which in its earlier stages was of a somewhat controversial character. BRITISH GRAVES IN EGYPT.—The Marquis of HARTING- TON said that the Egyptian Government had undertaken to provide a cemetery at Tel-el-Kebir for the graves of our soldiers and sailors who died in the late campaign. ARABI PASHA.—Lord :EDMUND FITZMAURICE stated that the Egyptian Government allowed Arabi Pasha and his fellow exiles in Ceylon £3O a mouth each, and expressed a willingness to increase the sum if found insufficient. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Sir J. M'Kenna, and was continued at some length by the Irish members.—Mr. PAR- NELL contented that the emigration policy of the Govern- ment was one that would render them infamous in the minds of the Irish people. He suggested that the judicious expenditure of £150,000, which could be obtained from the Church Surplus Fund, would save thousands from slow starvation. Neither emigration nor rnigiation would be any remedy for the immediate danger with which they are now threatened. An hour before midnight a division was taken upon Mr. O'Connor's amendment, which was rejected by a majority of 163 to 32.—After some further discussion, the Address to Her Majesty was agreed to.

BLUE RIBBON ARMY MEETING.—On Wednesday evening last, an entertainment was held in the Mission lent, Legh. street, in connection with the Blase Ribbon and Gospel Tern. perance movement. There' was a T.-ty good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. E. J. I Weaver. After the meeting had been opened, Mr. Jameson delivered an excellent address. Miss E. Broster then recited

" I should like to die, said Willie," and Mr. Weaver fol- lowed with the song "The dying girl to her mother." A. recitation, entitled "Don't smoke," was given by Miss E. Houghton, after which Miss S. A. Lackland recited "Poor Ned." "An interesting picture of drunkenness" was read by Mr. R. Sephton, and "Knock off those chains," by Mrs. Mullens. After Mr. E. Roden had excellently read "The pawnshop" (for which he received an encore), Mr. Weaver addressed the meeting, which concluded with the Benediction.

THREE CHARGES AGAINST ONE MAN.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Mills was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Havdock on the 10th February, and was fined ss. and costs.—He was also charged with assaulting and beating his wife Jane Mills on the same day; and further with stealing a coat, vest, and a pair of trousers, value 3ds. the property of William Corless.—The Prisoner: It's all a family affair and I plead guilty. It is my step-son--and I have been 40 years in the district and never been in this position before.—Superintendent Weir stated that the prisoner married the mother of Corless. The articles were placed in a box in the house, and they were afterwards missed. The prisoner sold the goods.—The prisoner: I was in drink and I did not know what I was doing.—Mrs. Mills (the pri- soner's wife): He struck me on the face.—The prisoner: I have only been two months married.—Mrs. Mills: I have been in bed two days because of his violence.—The pri- soner: I have been 31 years a sailor and have been on shore for eight years now. I was married two months ago yester- day and lam very sorry for what has happened. If you will only deal leniently with this case it shall never occur again.—Tbe Bench imposed a fine of 20s. and costs for the assault and robbery. div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY

THE CHANNEL TUNNEL.—There was a brief discussion on the Channel Tunnel question.—Earl GRANVILLE re- peated the statement made in the House of Commons that a joint committee would be appointed to consider the sub- ject, and said he thought it would not be desirable that any communication should be made to the French Government at the present time.—The Marquis of SALtsnunv asked if the question was not one of the class of political questions which the Government had always been held to be com- petent to decide on their own responsibility. It was a con- stitutional question of no -little magnitude, but he had no wish at that moment to discuss it at length. SCOTCH REPRESENTATIVE PEERS.—The Lord Chancellor brought in a bill founded on the recommendation of a Select Committee of 1881 and 1882 with reference to the election of representative peers of Scotland, and it was read a first time.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. ENGLAND AND PORTUGAL—The UNDER-SECRETARY for Foreign Affairs, in reply to Mr. Forster, said negotiations had been for some time in progress between this country and Portugal with respect to the Portugese claim of sorreignty over the banks of the Congo and certain adjoin- ing districts. The Government had no intention of taking the House by surprise in the matter. Full information would be given in the papers that would be laid on the table, but no decision had yet been arrived at. THE OFFICE OF PUBLIC PROSECUTOR.—The ATTORNEY. GENERAL informed Sir G. Campbell that no decision had been come to as to the re-organisation of the office of public prosecutor.—Sir G. CAMPBELL with a view of strengthening the bands of her Majesty's Government in dealing with this subject, gave notice that he would move, after the second reading of the Criminal Procedure Bill, that it be an instruction to the committee to inform themselves as to the law of Scotland in relation to public prosecution, so as to secure that in the United Kingdom the prosecution for serious offences should be an official, not a private duty. THE GOVERNMENT AND THE OPPOSITION.—Lord HAR- TINGTON declined to give Sir Stafford Northcote a day for the discussion of his motion on the Kilmainham Treaty. He stated that the remarks be made the other night were not intended in the sense in which they were taken up by the Opposition. It was far from his intention to comment unfairly on the action of the Opposition. The subject had been discussed on Mr. Gorst's motion, which was supported by the Opposition. Another motion for a Select Committee would, in the opinion of the Government, revive and keep open a controversy extremely embarrassing to the Irish Go- vernment, and prejudicial to the interests of order in Ireland. Besides, the state of public business made further discussion very iuconvenient.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE ex- pressed surprise at the decision of the Government in making challenges without meaning them to be taken up. He would take time to consider the course he should take. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS: MR. PARNELL'S AMENDMENT.—The debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. PARNELL, who proposed an amendment condemning the administration of the Crimes Act as tyrannical and unjust. The hon. member stated that the Government lost a very great opportunity after the Phcenix Park murders of restoring peace and order in Ireland by enlisting the aid and sympathy of. the people, instead of which they had recourse to the most drastic and tyrannical Act than had ever been passed, even for Ireland. The effect of this blunder was that there was never in Ireland greater hostility tw 'English rule, never a greater disinclination to aid in the maintenance of law and order, and the decrease of offences was only due to the the fact that the Government were keeping down the people by a tratal and a terlible Coercion Act. He strongly denounced the clauses in the Act giving the 'power of empanelling special juries; and asserted that thc conduct of the Irish judges had ntil been of a judicial character. During the administration e: the Crimes Act tbcre had been more scandals within a shorter space of time than ever before. There was no differ- ence, said the hon.Aentleman, between Lord Spencer at the head of his dragocns and the Czar wit.h his military eseort. except perhaps that the latter might have the majority of the people of Russia in his favour, while the Irish Govern- ment was universally detested in 'lreland. Until the Tesult of the judicial proceedings pending in Ireland had been ascertained they were not entitled to give an opinion as to whether there bad been an assassination society, ba there had been no attempts at outrage between May and November, when the attempt upon Mr. Justice Lawson took place, and it -was not until the extraor- dinary conduct of Mr. Justice Lawson in attack- ing the High Sheriff of the city of Dublin and the extra- ordinary way in which he conducted the trials-in Dublin that there came "this unhappy and wretched and lament- able recurrence of the attempts which had been alluded to as having been made by the so-called assassination societies." Reconciliation had been postponed or many a long year, but the problem would come up again, "What are you to do to reconcile Ireland to Englandl" He urged them instead of bringing in bankruptcy and municipal bills, about which nobody cared very much, to once more endeavour to settle the land -question. If then were only 5,000,000 of Irish, they had the sympathy of many millions of Irishmen in other countries, and with the aid of Irish- Americans they had the guarantee of ultimate success.— The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for IRELAND contended that the hon. member had not adduced a single case of positive hardship or injustice under the Crimes Act. The right hon. member defended the Irish Judges, and said though there might be some discontent in Ireland, he believed it would become quite and peaceable sooner than the hon. member e,q3ected. After remarks from Mr. Kenny and Colonel Dawnay, Mr. OSBORNE MORGAN contradicted the statement of Mr. Paraell as to the partiality of juries, stating that he was present during the trial of Walsh, and he could iron,: his experience of juries in this country say emphatically that he never be- held a more impartial jury, or a jury more indulgent to a prisoner. 'No person ever had a fairer trial, and at its close he remarked to Mr. Jnstice Lawson that-if that was the way they packed juries in Ireland he wished English juries could be packed in the same way.—Mr. A ARNOLD expressed his belief that if crime ceased in Ireland and agitation became lawful and reasonalde, government in Ireland would be pos- sible, and the country would go forward. The debate was continued by Dr. Commins, Mr. Plunket, Mr. O'Brien, Mr. Chaplin, and Mr. T. D. Sullivan. Upon a division Mr. Parnell's amendment was rejected by 133 to 15. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TCESDAY. .

A Bill introduced by -the Earl of GALLOWAY to amend the procedure at elections of representative peers of Scotland was read a first time.—On the motion of the Earl of BEL- MORE, the return of the Landed Estates Ccurt (Ireland) to the order of the 3rd Ju1y,.1882, was ordered to be continued, so as to include the sales for the year ending 31st December, 1882.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TrESDAr. DIE COMMITTEE OF SELECTION.—A long discussion ensued on the composition of the Committee of Selection.— On the motion of Sir JOHN MOWBRAY, the House agreed, after some discussion, to increase the membership of the committee from five to seven, 3 proposition by Mr. rARNELL that Mr. Justin VCarthy should be added to the committee instead of Mr. Mitchell Henry being rejected by 157 against
NEW MEMBER.-Mr. John Morley was introduced by Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Mr. Buar, and took his seat for New- castle amid Ministerial cheers.

. - AG ruccLrußAL GrawrascEs.—The agricultural repre- sentatives strongly opposed a motion for the second reading of a Scotch railway bill on the ground that it sought to impose exceptionally high charges for the carriage of arti- ficial manures, a new departure" which it was considered would be detrimental to the interests of agriculture. The PRESIDENT of the Board of Trade undertook that the at- tention of the Committee should be specially called to the question of rates, but this did not satisfy Mr. E. STANHOPE, at whose instance the debate was adjourned for a week. THE RELPASE OF MEMBERS FROM KILMAINHAM. Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE announced his intention to ask the Prime Minister on Monday for facilities in reference to his motion touching the Kilmainham negotiation—On the mo- tion for nostponing the orders of the day, Mr. R. YonrEE complained of the remarks of Lord Hartington in reference to his action respecting the inquiry into the Kilmainham Teeaty.—The Marquis of HARTINGTON deprecated taking up time discussing the question now, in view of the appeal to he made on Monday, and declined to follow Mr. Yorke through the history of the motion.—After some further remarks, the motion was postponed, and the orders of the day were agreed to. THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS: IRISH DISTRESS.—The adjourned debate on the Address was resumed by Mr. A. O'CONNOR, who moved an amendment relating to the dis- tress in Ireland. The debate was continued by Colonel Colthurst,Mr. J. M'Carthy, Mr. Charles Russell, Sir J. Hay, and Mr. Trevelyan.—The CHIEF SECRETARY mentioned the measures the Gevernment intended to introduce for Ireland, and added that they thought it undesirable to go on pouring out public money which did not advantage either the Exchequer or Ireland, but that they should be doing much belt., by encouraging in the Irish people self-reliance at home and by giving assistance without compulsion to those who wished to go elsewhere. After remarks from Mr. Gibson, Mr. O'Connor Power, Mr. Forster, and Mr. Callan, the debate was adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

THE DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.—The adjourned debateoPl the Address was resumed. Several Irish members con- demned the scheme for promoting emigration from Ireland, and advised a plan of migration instead.—Mr. CORRY main- tained that tke best cure for the distress was emigration.— Mr. BLAKE recommended emigration to British America. . _ .

The immigrants, he said, would be treated with infinitely more consideration by the Dominion Government and the people than they would receive in the United States.—Mr. T. Dicitsoli advocated a judicious use of migration and emigration.—Mr. CHILDERS spoke of the wide differences of opinion existing as to the cure for Irish distress, and said ' the Government were making inquiries with the object of arriving at the proper remedy. The right hon. gentleman appealed to the House to bring the debate to a close that day, so that the business of Supply might be proceeded with.—Several speeches, however, followed that of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and Mr. Callan was address- ing the House when the time arrived for the adjournment of the debate.—The Marquis of HARTINGTOII gave notice that the Government proposed that on the conclusion of the debate the ouse should proceed at once with the report of the Address.
