div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TIIIIRSDAY.
The Hoas—e -sat for Only a quarter of an hour, the ro- ceedings being limited to a notiee by Lord Cranbrook to ask the Secretary of the Colonies as to the damages re-

div.head: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
div.p: FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,
A. Durban telegram reports a complete victory by the Transvaal Boers over the chief Mapoch. .

A village in Sweden has been so completely gutted by fire that only 32 chimneys are left standing. A family council of the Orleans princes was held on Mon- day, at the residence of the Due de Chartres, Paris, to discuss the situation. It is reported that the princes have decided to appeal to the Cornell of State against the decree depriv- ing them of their commands in the army. The "outrage " upon an Italian at Tripoli has been amply atoned for. The Governor-General of the Province has paid a formal visit to the Italian Consul in order to express regret for the insult to his countryman. The Italian community are said to be much pleased with the settlement of the difficulty. A tariff question, which affects the carriage of sulphur, has given rise to disorderly scenes at Catania. The Italian Governraent has strongly reinforced the garrison, and numerous arrests have been made. Catania is largely in- terested in the sulphur trade, and the people allege that new rates which are being levied by the public compasies seri- ously affect their interests. "General" Booth is including Southern Afri,:a in the sphere of his operations. A Reuter's telegram reports the arrival at Capetown of a detachment of the" Army." They 'ere received, of course, by an excited crow, and some ttirring news may be looked for on the outbreak of " hos- 'tilities" among the colonists. It is not stated that the Sail- - vationists intend to go north, where the Pondos and the Xesibes are at war, and are daily expected to fight a very sanginuary battle. M. de Brazza is not to tie allowed to recommence his ." explorations" without sufficient protection. The Minister of War has placed at his service a full company of Algerian sharpshooters, together with a quantity 01 arms for the defence of the stations he proposes to establish. The supply consists of t,OOO percussion muskets, 20,00 C swords, 100,000 kilogrammes of powder, 10,0-50,000 caps, 230 tents, and 1,000 hatchets. The vessel which the Minister of War has appointed for the Mee of the expedition can ".?, taken to pieces, so that where navigation is not practicable t need not be abandoned.

The question of the Governor Generalship of the Lebanon is attracting much attention at Constantinople. The term of office of the present Governor, Rustem Pasha, has nearly expired, and his re-appointment is strongly opposed by the French Ambassador. The representatives of England, Aus- tria, Russia and cltaly favour the confirmation of Rustem in his office, Germany remaining neutral. The Times corres- pondent at Constantinople says that a new complication seems to be dawning in Eastern affairs, and hints that "dis- turbances could at any time be fomented by the numerous French partisans in Syria." MYSTERIOUS DEATH OF AN ANGLO•IITDIAN.—Some ex- citement has been caused in the Punjaub by the sudden and mysterious death at Jurnmoo of Mr. Johnstone, an Eng- lish gentleman, who for some years held high office in the service of the Maharajah of Cashmere. Some notes written by Mr. Johnstone after he had been taken ill showed that be believed himeelf to have been poisoned. Sir Oliver St. John went frorruSealkote to Jurnmoo to investigate the matter, and brought to Lahore a bottle of whisky some of the contents of which Mr. Johnstone had drunk shortly be- fore his death. A chemical analysis proved that ths bottle contained a mixture of whisky, ether, andshloroform. The mystery is still unsolved. - •

- - SECRET SOa.RTIE-5 ,ON THE CONTlNENT.—lmportant arrests following an explosion of dynamite have been made in the neighbourhood of Brussels. Two men, one of whom was mortally wounded, are in custody, and it is stated that both were recently sentenced for taking part in the distur- bances at Montceau les Mines. One of the men, Metayer, has made important confessions at the preliminary inquiry before the Judge d'lnstruction. The police have seized a number of documents which it is said reveal the existence of a conspiracy affecting not only Belgium but several European States. At Cracow much sensation has been created by the arrest of a number of students at the University, who are charged with Socialist intrigues. The authorities in Spain believe that they have obtained valuable information as to the organisa- tion of the secret societies recently discovered in Andalusia. The objects of the societies are set forth in the statutes to be the complete destruction of the rights of property, the ex- termination of the bourgeoisie and wealthy landowners by all means in their power, especially by fire, assassination, and poison. Among the crimes traced to these societies are agrarian outrages, incendiarism, destruction of crops and cattle, and attacks on bakers' shops. The detection of the ringleaders arose from two murders which were accom- plished, and another which was Vanned by secret assassina- tion societies in Jerez.

. day —e Dracheta of Albany gave birth to a claugbkor on Sull- evr.ming. b, house at Ecclefechata, in which Carlyle was born, has aU purchased by his niece, Mrs. Carlyle. 4obn Milne, aged 17, undergoing 18 months' imprison- latent at Perth, has hanged himself in his cell. The Press Association is informed by the Astronomer atoYal that a new comet has been discovered in America. _ The 'Victoria Music Hall, Grimsby, was destroyed by re ort Sunday morning. There had been a performance overnight. The Rev. J. F. Thorpe, vicar of Herne Hill, ivhile preach- mg at Seasalter Church on Sunday night suddenly fainted _and died in a few minutes. The incident caused a painful eensation among the congregation. Salisbury election petition has failed. On Monday the iudges delivered judgment forthe respondents, without costs, ao that Ma. Coleridge Kennard retains his seat. Three Persons will be reported as guilty of bribery. toll. mill at Sowerby Bridge belonging to the Clough Mill th:PanY, and occupied by Messrs. Greenwood and Crow: blanket manufacturers, was destroyed by fire on at,-r-aw morning The loss of property is estimated at -aunt E 20,000. The Council of the National Amalgamated Society of tr,ertworkers are taking steps towards restricting the output 9,t finished iron. They have passed a resolution declaring that sliding scales for the regulation of wages are useless risks means are taken to prevent the glutting of the mar- et and reckless under-selling. ~T11_,13 QUEEN ARE JESSIE ACE.—The Queen, in acknow- , "aging the receipt of a portrait of Miss Jessie Ace, the r!eroic rescuer of two of the shipwrecked crew of the barque ilrinz Adalbert on the 27th of last month, states that she is greatly pleased with the photograph both as a work of art and as a memento of a noble act. The photograph was eriPplied at the express request of Her Majesty. A COLLIERY FLoonEn.—The bed of the river Sheaf, at a Point where it flows under the Midland Railway Station at Sheffield, has fallen in for a short distance, and water at the rate of 2,000 to 3,000 gallons a minute has been making its way into the workings ot the Nunnery Colliery. The discovery was made on Saturday. It is believed that much damage has been done to the workings. ATTEMPTED DOIIBLE MURDER.—A desperate attempt at double murder was committed on Saturday night at Beeston, by a man named James Johnson, a designer and draughts- man, who has only recently returned to England from Australia. He had a married sister named Waplington living at Beeston, it is said, with a man not her husband, aed he was so enraged at this that be shot them both. The !roman is dangerously wounded in the thigh, and both are In a critical condition. ENGLAND AND THE TRANSYALL.--A parliamentary paper gives an estimate of the amount required in the year ending ~,March 31st next, for defraying expenses connected with the Transvaal. This shows that the total is £14,000, as com- Pared with £400,000 in the previous financial year, a decrease of £386,000. The heads of the estimate are £4,312, charges connected with the annexation in 1877; £1,726 expenses of commissions, £940 compensation awards, 4,1,023 liabilities of the late Colonial Government. CALEDONIAN RAILWAY Sicavarrs.—A meeting of Cale- donian railway servants was held in Edinburgh on Sunday. A. resolution was passed, declaring the general manager's circular in reply to the workmen's petition in effect a flat denial, conceding nothing, and showing a determination to oract the same exorbitant hours as formerly. The men agreed to approach the company with a proposal to submit disputed questions to arbitration, being convinced that the present dissatisfied state of the staff render the bar- Monious conducting of traffic impossible. SUPPLEMENTARY EstrmarEs.—A•supplementary estimate Lot Civil Services and Revenue Department basbeen issued. the total sum required is £516,555. Of this 120,000 is for stationery and printing, £40,000 for law charges and criminal Prosecutions, £45,000 for Irish Land Commission, £33,000 10r Dublin police, £42,000 for education for England and Wales, £31,000 for diplomatic services, and £239,000 for Post office and telegraphs. A note to the account of the t efira required for Irish law charges says that the addi- tional expense incurred is. owing to the disturbed state of tue country. • BRUTAL MURDER'BY 'FATITEIL—David Urquhart, 33 Years of age, went to his house in Hilltown, Dundee; late on Saturday night, in a ball-drunken state. He had more !iquor, and then quarrelled with his wife, who took refuge lo a neighbour's house to escape from his violence. The marl -then attacked his children, three of whom, aged nreePectively four, two, and one years. were in the house. 'arm of the children, Lavina, aged four years, waribeaten to death, and another little one was so badly injared that it is „ expected to recover. After evading the police for several mays, Urquhart gave himself up. LONDON IRISHMEN AND MR. FORSTER.—A • sparsely- attended meeting of Irishmen was held on Clerkenwell Green, London, on Sunday afternoon, at which resolutions y„were passed condemning the speech of Mr. Forster in the unase of Commons on Thursday as detrimental to good government and tending to weaken the good feeling which ought to exist between England and Ireland, and calling iflPen• the Government to order that the men awaiting trial Or „ t --h ePhcenix Park and other murders should be tried by - Pry legitimately formed of Irishmen, and.not by a com- mission of jukes. One of the speakers alluded to Mr. Forster as " the most miserable hound that ever lived." AN OFFICER SHOT ON A PARADE GROUND.—A de- Dlorable occurrence has resulted in the death of Lieutenant William Holland Coode, second son of General Coode, of Devouport. The deceased was an officer in the Lincolnshire regiment, quartered at Benares. On Friday he was shot uead on the parade ground, whether accidentally or in- tentionally is unknown. Lieutenant Coode was adjutant, and would superintend the drills, but the men would only be furnished with blank cartridges, except at target practice. T„..be unfortunate officer entered the army four years ago. Re was of fine physique. 24 years of age, 6ft. 3in. in height, and of a remarkably amiable and cheerful disposition. THE STOCKPORT MURDER : CONFESSION OF THE PRI- -B"ER.—The Stockport Coroner (Mr. F. W. Johnson) on Saturday resumed the inquest on the body of James Moores, Who was brutally murdered on the 13th inst. at the Meadow Mill, Portwood. James Robert Price, the man charged with the Crime, was present in custody. The prisoner, it ap- Peered, had made a statement to the police in the presence of his brother, in which he confessed that he had struck the deceased on the bead with an axe. He added .that he did not mean to kill Moores, with whom be never had a wrong I;rord, but he "mistook the man." No motive was given 3r his haying committed the act, unless, as suggested by the Coroner in summing up the evidence to the jury, the Prisoner had some hope of getting the situation held by his The jury returned a verdict of wilful murder against Price, and he was committed for trial on the Coroner's warrant.

EXTRAORDINARY APPEAL Casg.—ln the Court of Appeal GO Monday, before the Master of the Rolls, Sir Jas. Hannen, and Lord Justice Bowen, an extraordinary ease was heard, Viz., that of Hind v. Brett and others. It was an appeal from the decision of Vice-Chancellor Hall refusing to enter- tain the plaintiff's claim, and the defendants were Lords Justices Brett, Baggallay, Cotton, and Brindley, and Mr. Justices Manisty, Lopes, and Stephens. The plaintiff Claimed £6,000 damages from the defendants for illegal acts, for omitting to perform official functions, for obstructing and defeating the course of justice, for acting with injustice, °PPression, and partiality, for abusing their powers, and authorising wrong and injury to the plaintiff. The appellant, who appared in person, now asked leave to amend his writ Ted claim damages for trespass. He complained that Lord Justice Brett had stopped his appeal against the Speaker of the House of Commons. The court dismissed the appeal With costs, and refused leave to amend the writ. b CIaMING A STORM : SUCCESSFUL USE OF OIL AT SEA.— articulare have been received on the voyage of the Liver- -1)201 steamer Stanmore, from Swansea to New York. She Zt Swansea on the 18th January, and all went well until ga? reached lat. 48, long. 32, whe3 she encountered a heavy e' which -soon developed into a hurricane. The docks Were sivept so repeatedly with the heavy seas that the crew '.„-`_re obliged to lash themselves to the riggings. The gale 7°ll afterwards abated, but on reaching the banks of New- foundland another storm arose, and -during its height the rain steampipe of the vessel burst. This left tlie ship help- es, and she fell into the trough of the- sea. Fortunately the master, Captain Athorni, bethought himself that he had a quantity of oil-on board, and be filled some bags with it and put them ever the vessel's side. In a few seconds the waves ceased to break over the ship, the sea became much quieter, and the repairs to the steampipe were successfully -effected, the result being that Ahe:Stanmore was able to pro- ceed on her voyage next day, anti she arrived at New York on the Bth inst. From this it appears that out of a population of -25,968.286 the number convicted amounted to 15;921, and that 10,901 of them were 60.taficlis residents in the district where the apprehensions were made. WE have this week been favoured with two notable after-dinner speeches one from Lord CRANBROOK, a distinguished member of the Upper House ; and:the other from Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, the free lance of the Lower Chamber. The remarks of Lord CRANBROOK are noticeable chiefly because of the alarmist view he takes of political ques- tions generally at the present time, but more especially of our Indian policy; while the' utterances of Lord CHURCHILL are remarkable mainly for their wholesale abuse of the Go- vernment. The former noble lord fouad an opportunity to deliver his observations at the annual dinner of the Westminster Conservative Association ; the latter disgorged himself amongst his own constituents at Woodstock. Lord CRAN BROOK was a trusted member of the late Cabinet, in which he filled the post of Secretary of State for India, and this latter fact will account for the apparently excessive zeal with which he watches over our Indian possessions. The fear of Russian aggression which haunted the noble lord when in office and precipitated us in the Afghan war seems to follow him still, hence we find him warn- ing his hearers and the country of the Russian tide that is flowing unceasingly in Central Asia, and advancing on the mountains that form the boundaries of our great Indian Empire. The noble lord is not bold enough to say that Russia will invade India, he leaves that to be inferred; but he does say it is only by keeping up the feeling that England is predominant and all powerful, and that there is no greater power than that of Britain, that we can maintain our position. Once, he says further, let the feeling go abroad that there is a Power greater than England and more powerful, and then there will be talk in the bazaars that the sun of England is going to set ! Now, what we should like to know is the good of alarmist talk such as this? What useful purpose can it serve? Our Indian Empire is not assailed at any point, the Russian hordes which Lord CRANBROOK when in office saw advancing at every turn are still a far way off, and until we have reasonable grounds for believing that Russia really has aggressive designs upon our Indian possessions, we should be acting unwisely in paying any heed to the anti-Russian preju- dices of the late Secretary. ik distrust of Russia is still predominant in the minds of the leading Opposition Statesmen, it was this uncalled for distrust which embarked us in the Afghan war with its consequent blood- shed and waste of money, and it is revived now in the hope of creating an anti-Russian feeling throughout the country, such as was experienced some years ago when the Tories were in power. Surely the Statesmen now at the helm of Indian affairs are not less alive to our interests in India than Lord CRANBROOK and his friends; if anyone is foolish enough to suppose so we need only point to the Egyptian war, one of the chief reasons for undertaking which was to prevent the Suez Canal getting into the possession of a hostile Power, and so jeopardising our road to India. Lord CRANBROOK is alarmed, too, at the legislation which we are promised. He believes it will be legislation of destruction and construction, and, conjuringup in his mind a host of imaginary difficulti?.s, calls upon the people to be prepared to meet them. Here Lord CRANBROOK tries to enlighten his hearers upon something in which he himself must be in a state of blissful ignorance, for the details of the forthcoming legislation have not yet been disclosed. It will, however, we may safely say, be destructive only in the sense that it will do away with that which is found to be unsuited to the present time and circumstances ; and it will be constructive inasmuch as it will be designed to meet the pressing and proved wants of the country. The speech of Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL is, as we have said, remarkable for its abuse of the Government. The noble lord is well known to be a master of invective, but in the present instance he appears to have surpassed him- self. We hear every now and again of the violent language indulged in by the Irish members, and the recent attack of Mr. PARNELL On Mr. FORSTER has been very strongly condemned; but Lord RANDOLPH —this scion of the nobility—has eclipsed even Mr. PARNELL'S course vituperation The member for Woodstock condemns the Government for what he calls their neglect of agricultural interests, though we deny there has been any such neglect. As a matter of fact the measures to benefit the

agriculturalist passed by Mr. GLADSTONE'S Government far surpass those placed on the statute book by the late Administration; but at the same time the complaint is one which, if he thinks the Government has neglected these interests, the noble Lord is entitled to make. Leaving, however, the region cf, what is legitimate criticisin, all parties whatever be their political faith—must agree I in censuring the unmeasured and most 1 unjustifiable language which Lord RA....Nnouni gave expression to with regard to other matters. The truth, he said, of the present political situation was that we had to do with a Government of imposture, an administra- tiori of make-believes, whose every act was either a fraud or a sham. He declared that on the 4th May last the government of Ireland was handed over to Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN, the caucus-monger of Birmingham, and to Mr. SHERIDAN, the outrage-monger of I Tubbercurry ; and if it had not been for those 1 terrible murders in the Phcenix Park the destinies of that unhappy country might still be in the hands of those two temporary accomplices. The Government, individually and collectively we suppose, are a "set of detected political imposters," they obtained ! their power by fraud and falsehood, they had exercised it for wrong and robbery, and they must resign it ere long in unutterable degra- dation and unmeasurable infamy. Though I this is a species of abuse to which the . Government are becoming accustomed, it also belongs to that category of political war- fare which is very much to be deprecated. Course and vulgar denunciation hurled . at gentlemen who are certainly not less honourable than any of the occupants of the Opposition benches can only recoil upon the person making use of it. Abuse is no argu- ment whatever, and it betrays a very weak cause indeed when it has to be resorted to. ' It may go down very well with an audience in a state of political darkness, but to the intelligent reader the language and the speaker will alike be appraised at their true I value. It is fortunate for the noble lord. that he selected Woodstock to let off his thunderbolts; had he offered to discharge them in St. Stephens, he would have been very quickly called to account by the I SPEAKER, Lord RANDOLPH, by his last extra-parliamentary utterance, must have seriously damaged himself in the eyes of his political allies, as he most surely has lowered himself in the estimation of his countrymen. At a time when Parliamentary business is becoming somewhat dry and tedious extra- parliamentary deliverances are welcomed, as a sort of relief; but we fear that speeches such I as those we have referred to, instead of , diffusing a healthy political rivalry in debate'l are calculated to create a, desire to evade it, and to work considerable mischief.

. . I will shortly have to decide, To to Mr. EGERTON'S only qualification seems to be that he is. an EGERTON, and no doubt he thinks he has a prescriptive right to the seat. He states he is a member of the Metropolitan , Board of Works, but that is no qualification whatever. It is certainly one reason why the farmers of Mid-Cheshire should not elect I him, for it shows that he is not resident in 1 their midst, and not likely to be. He is I comparatively unknown in the constituency, he has never done anything for the electors in the past, and it is questionable whether he will do anything in the future, even if elected. On the other hand, the electors have in Mr. LATHAM an old and tried friend, one who has always taken a deep interest in every question affecting the farmer, and for his bold advocacy of their claims he has frequently been made to suffer in his social relations. By electing Mr. LA.THAM the electors of Arid-Cheshire will do honour to him and an honour to themselves, and they will be sending ta the House of Com- mon a gentleman whose council and advice on all questions affecting argriculture will be valued even \ there.

This Bil: came before the Standing Orders Committee of the House o 2 Commons yesterday, in consequence of the Examiners of Private Bills having report?,d non-compliance with Standing. Orders in reference to the depositing of plans of certain work proposed to be done on the Upper Mersey. The committee, who sat in private, decided to allow the Bill to go on this session ; but they struck out the first half of clause 26, which empowers the promoters to make the works refeired to, and of which plans have not been deposited. The portion of the clause struck out gave the promoters the power of dredging, scouring, opening, deepen- ing, cleansing, straightening, and widening the beds, banks, and channels of the Upper. Mersey. The • effect of the decision will be that the promoters, is 3accessful in getting their Bill through this session, will have to come to Parliament 'again next session for the powers- which were struck out of the Bill yesterday.

CRESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE BlLL.—.This bill came before Mr. Examiner Robinson in the House of Commons o i Monday. The bill seeks to confer further powers on the committee, and proofs were given that it had received the approval of the N-arious companies interested at special Wharncliffe meetings. The further standing orders of Parliament were therefore declared to have been complied with.

WSDNES SCHOOL BOLRD AT Wonir.---The followireg per- sons were each fined ss. st Widnes Petty Sessions, ore Wed- nesday, for breaches of the Education Act-:-Thotnas Prescot, Wm. Smith, Joseph Coppock (two 'cases), !Cary Hayes, Thomas McCord, , Eden Williams, Edward Jerks, Wm. Worthington, John Joht-Aon, John Dillon (two cases), Michael McDermott, Thomas WelSh, Richard Williams, James Handy, and John Kelly. ' A RUNCORN GAOL BIHD.—At the Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Catherine Bowden was charged with wil- fully damaging the dwelling-house occupied by Samuel Ashton.—On Saturday night the defendant's husband was visiting at the carnplainant's house, when the defendant, who wished him to come out, sent mugs, buckets, and other missies flying through the windows,smashing2o panes of glass and the frame. The damage was estimated at £l.—Supt. Williamson said the prisoner had spent the last two years and nine months in gaol, and the Bench fined her £1 and costs and ordered her to pay the damage, or, in default, a month's hard labour.—The defendant expressed her willing- ness to go for the month. TEE RUNCORN HARRIERS.—The first meet of this club took place on Saturday, and a very pleasant run was en- joyed. The hares, Messrs. C. Leach and T. Horsfall, started from Union-street at 2-30, five minutes start being allowed them and:they made in the direction of Rock Savage. They quickly left Halton Grange on the left, and made a dash for the Flood Brooks. From thence they proceeded smartly through Sutton, and here doubled in the direction of Dutton, the bounds in full cry. After some heavy running to bares gained the shelter of Murdershire Wood. and here left the hounds a little and proceeded in the ;Erection of Norton Wood and up to Halton. While the hares were being re- freshed at the Castle Hotel, the hounds suddenly appeared on the hill, and a close race now took place, T. Horsfall be- ing caught in Halton Fields. 'Rogers being within a short distance of the other hare, an exciting race ensued, the bare eventually winning by about 30 yards. . _

DROWNED IN -A DOCK AT RUNCORN.—At the Board- room of the Burial Board, Cemetery, on Monday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquiry into the circumstance of the death of Adam Grundy, a fiatman, 35 years of age, who resided at Astley.—From the evidence of a waterman, named Heathcote, living at Marple, it appeared that deceased was mate on the flit John, belonging to Mr. Richard Baxter. On Saturday night the fiat was lying in the tidal dock at Runcorn, and about 20 minutes to eleven the deceased, Who had been in the town, went on board in a state of drunkenness. He told Heathcote that be would go forward and go to bed. A few minutes afterwards some men raise& an alarm that there was a man in the water, and the canal watchman, James Weedall, obtained the grappling irons. A hat was handed to him, which be believed belonged to the deceased, and he went to the flat. Heathcote then discovered that the deceased had not gone to bed as he stated he should do so. A small boat was obtained, and in a few minutes the dead body of the de- ceased was recovered from the water.—A verdict of " Accidental death " was recorded. STAR. OF TEMPERANCE BRASS BAND, WFDNES.—With the object of defraying the cost of new uniform for this body of instrumentalists a concert was given in the Volun- teer Hall, on Saturday evening last, when there was a large audience present. The Rev.,G. Bond, vicar of Farnwortb, presided. The band performed their part of the programme in theft usual tastetul style, while Mr. Morris, who sang "The midshipmite " and "Goodwin sands," was highly successful. Mrs. Rushton was encored for her rendering of the "Sad sea waves," and a similar compliment rewarded her for the song, "Molly Bawn." Mr. J. R. Lea sang, with fine spirit, " The old brigade," and he also gave in capital style " The powder monkey." "The ash grove," a clarionet solo, by Mr. W. Kay, was per- formed with taste, and "Where is the rover," by Miss A.. White was encored. Mr. Greenhough was heard to advant- age in "Alice, where art thou ?" and "Madeline "; while a splendid success was achieved by Messrs. Alf. Davies and F. W. Wareing in the comic duet, "By-and-bye," which con- tained a number of local allusions which were very amus- ing. The programme also included "Love's request," by Mr. J. H. Bury; pianoforte solo, "Battle march of Delhi,"' by Master R. Briggs; "Bridget Muldoon," Mr. A. Ga Davies; Mr. Bury," I wish thi mother would come," &c. AN INTERESTING WIDNES RATE CASE.—MT. Gough, the assistant overseer, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, and applied for an immediate order upon the London and North-Western Railway Company for the pay- ment of £22 3s. 11d., the arrears of a poor rate laid in Feb., 1881, and for £2B 10s. 9d., the arrears of a poor rate laid on the let March, 1832. Mr. Gough said the company had appealed against the assessment, but the Assessment Committee had upheld it; Mr. Howard, who represented the company, said that when the first rate was made upon the company, there were two items relating to an engine shed. This shed had been pulled down, but the overseers had ommitted to strike the item out. Anew abed was erected upon the site of the old one. Before the new building was completed, he (Mr. Howard) met the overseers, who said the company were clearly entitled to have the old item struck out, and to have an allowance made. ']he com- pany paid the rate in accordance with that arrangement, and received a receipt in discharge. Now they had a new claim in which the item for the demolished sited appeared as recoverable arrears, although one rate had been paid.— Mr. Gough said the overseers had no right to strike out an assessment until there was a new valuation made. The old assessment had been increased on account of the new addi- tion.—Mr. Qaskell said the Bench had no discretion in the matter, and an order for immediate payment was made. He informed Mr. Howard that the company's proper course was to appeal. AN EXTRAORDINARY ASSAULT CASIt AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Joseph Worth was ' brought up, on remand, charged with committing an aggravated assault upon Elizabeth Smith, a girl, 13 years of age, who lives with her parents in Titnperley-street. The charge was reduced to one of common assault.—Mr. J. 0. Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the prisoner.—From the evidence of the prosecutrix and her witnesses—Sarah White, of Midwood-street, and Mary Ellen Smith—it appeared that on Monday afternoon a crowd of upwards of a hundred persons were assembled in Timperley-street to watch a fight, when the prisoner and a companion, named Austin Young. were seen to come from the direction of a house of ill-fame in the neighbourhood. The crowd then apparently turned their attention to these two, and the prisoner picked up a stone which he threw. It struck the prosecutrix on be forehead, inflicting a wound 21 inches long, and tpenetrating to the bone. She was conveyed into the house of Mrs. White, and Dr. McLennan was called in and dressed the wound. According to the evidence of P.S. McGregor, the girl was in a very weak state, and was compelled to remain in bed all day on Tuesday. For the defence it was con- tended that the persons in the crowd were throwing stones at the prisoner and his companion, who were pursued to Appleton. Prisoner totally denied that he or Young sent a stone Mr. Swift said the prisoner had promised to pay the doctor's charges and compensate the parents of the injured girl if that would meet the wishes of the Bench.—The prisoner was fined £3 and costs. RUNCORN COFFEE AND COCOA HOUSE CO., LIMITED.— The annual meeting of this company was held in the rooms, High-street, on Monday afternoon. There were present— Messrs. J. 0. Jackson (in the chair), John Simpson, B. Kniveton, S. C. Beckett, T. Norman, Robert Norman, J. Meadowcroft, John Higgins. Owing to there not 'being a quorum present, business could not be proceeded with, and the meeting was adjourned until Monday next. The direc:ors report stated :—The directors are pleased to be able to announce to the shareholders that although the year's returns do not enable them to declare any dividend, 'yet there has been such an increase in the business, combined with a judicious reduction in the expenses, as to bring down the deficiency of last year from £4l 2s 5d to £5 16s Id, and to justify the hope that an equal amount of businessduring the present year will place a good balance in the hands of your directors at its close. The receipts for the year amount to £926 16s 3d, being an advance over the previous year. A glace at the balance sheet will show that the anticipations of your directors have been realised, by a considerable re- diiction having been effected in the bank charges. Whilst announcing that the financial results are more satisfactory, the directors are also pleased to know that the company continues to promote and increase habits of sobriety amongst that portion of the community for whose special conveni- ence and benefit it was established. A RAID ON WIDNES MILE SELLERS.—Before Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, sen., and Mr. G. Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions' on Wednesday, Benjamin Hughes, Hurst-street; James Peters, White-street; Mary Murphy, Ann-street West; Mary Holden, Widnes-road; John Ashton, Appleton; John Frost, Ann-street West; Wm. Barber, Lord-street; Richard Stinson, Charles-street; James Riley, Midwood-street ; Elizabeth McGee, Kent-street; Richard Garton, Appleton; Thomas Fisher, Warrington-road; Thomas Molloy, Victoria. street; Joshua Abbott, Milton-road; Jane Urquhart, Char- lotte-street; James Pace, 29, Irwell-street; were each sum- moned on a charge of carrying on the trade of purveyors of milk without being registered for that purpose.—Mr.Gaskell said the Bench were not disposed to fine the defendants, as they were of opinion that the local authority had not done their part. They had not in a reasonable and proper way brought the Act of Parliament under the notice e the milk sellers and others interested. They had failed to give the Bench evidence that they had even advertised the Act once in any newspaper circulated in the district since it was passed in 1879. All the cases would therefore be dismissed. Now the defendants knew what the law was, they musst apply for registration, and give the local authority the opportunity of seeing that their dairies, cow sheds' and houses were suitable and in proper condition. No doubt theta proceedings will be a warning to them, and to other milk dealers in the district, of the riqairements of the law. and he had no doubt they would comply alith them.—ln reply to a question from Superintendent Barker, Mr. Gaskell said the police bad done their duty; the local authority was in fault.

ASHTON.

FATAL ACCIDENT AT GATISWOOD COLLIERY.—On Friday last Mr. Barker, coroner, held an inquest at the Park Hotel, Park-lane, on the body of James Atherton, a collier, 60 years of age, residing at Lambhead Green, Pemberton, who met with his death under the following circumstances. The deceased was employed in the Garswood Coal and Iron Company's Colliery at Park-lane, and was at work at 9.45 on the morning of the previous Tuesday, when a large stone fell upon him from the roof. He was found with the stone on his head, the poor fellow being quite dead. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." EDDISBURY.

--„- • , DErRAUDING THE uHESHIRE LINES COMmITTEE: A DAIRY FARMER HEAVILY FINED.—At the Eddisbury Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Lord Tollemache and other magistrates, Peter Snelson, a farmer, of Manley Hall, Mouldsworth, was summoned by the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee for making a false statement in regard to the quanti- ties of milk sent by him by train from Mouldsworth to Manchester.—Mr. Hamp, solicitor to the Cheshire Lines Committee, in opening the ease, stated that in the month of January the stationmaster at Mouldsworth had reason to suspect that the cans of milk forwarded to Manchester by the defendint contained very much more than they were represented to contain in the consignment note. The cans were examined, and on the 23rd January it was found that the defendant filled his consignment notes for 22 gallons, whereas the consignee' ' Mr. Moore, of Manchester, would prove that he received 30 gallons on that day. A watch was kept, and it was found that during eight days in Janu- ary 90 gallons were under stated; that in February 66 gallons, making a total of 156 gallons.—Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, for the:defence, argued that the discrepancies, which he admitted, were due to mistake rather than to an intent to defraud. The defendant made up his consignment note at night, as the train started very early in the morning. —Mr. Hamp replied that the continued 4iscrepancies showed that there was systematic fraud.—There were 18 summonses against defendant, but one only was taken, and the Bench, considering the case proved, mulcted de- fendant in a penaly of £lO and costs, amounting altogether to £l7 Os. 4d.

NEGLECTING TO SEND CHILDREN TO SCHOOL.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturdry last, William Gilliker and Peter Canaan, labourers, were summoned for neglecting to send their children to school, as required by the Educa- tion Act.—Mr. Henry Pegg, school attendance ofncer, proved the charges, and each defendant was fined ss. HAYDOCK. A COLLIER AND HIS DRAWER: SINGULAR DISPUTE.— At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Atkinson claimed the sum of 10s from John Wright, alleged to be due as wages. The complainant stated that be was , the drawer for the defendant, who was a collier. On the 9th of February the defendant brought him his mousy for four days' work. He should, he said, be paid weekly at the rate of 5s 2d per day. 'On the date itkquestion he had four days' ' wages to draw, and the defendant gave him £1 Os 3d. He then went out of the house, but returned in a few minutes, and said he had given 103 too much. The defendant, how- ever, refused to give him the . Additional two days' wages when they were due.—Sarah Atkinson wife of the complainant stated that she was present when her husband was paid, and he only received £l. Os 23.—The defendant was then sworn, and he deposed that he gave the complainant 30s instead of ill Cts Bd. He had his own money in one pocket, and the complainant's in another, and with- out looking he gave the complainant his (defendant's) own money.--,The Bench dismissed the case, observing that they were afraid the complainant had got more money than be was entitled to. CAUGHT IN THE ACT OF STEALING A DUCK AT HAY- Winstanley, a collier, residing at New Poston, was brought before C. Pitkington,Esq ,at Haydock, on Thursday afternoon, and was remanded on a , charge of stealing a duck, value 35., the property of George Cawley, farmer. it appears that the prosecutor had a number of ducks on a pond near to his farm, and just before dusk one was missed. A seri of Mr. Cawley saw the prisonar run- ning away from the pond and followed him across the fields. Seeing he was likely for being caught, the prisoner dropped the duck, but young Cawley still kept up the pursuit, and ultimately secured the prisoner. P.C. Hodgkinson was on duty near at hand, and hearing someone whistling, pro- ceeded thereto, and took the prisoner into custody.

The annual sermons on behalf of the choir of Christ Church, Winsford (Weaver), were preached on Suaday last. The morning sermon by the Rev. Davis. Jones, M.A:, of Davenham, and in the evening by the Rev. ff.-0-.--Yettardp of Whitegate. The offertory amounted to :yearly £4. FATAL SALT ACCIDENT AT WINSFORD.—A man named Hodkinson, of Over, who worked at Messrs. Verdin's works, Winsford, fell into the boiling brine on Monday. He scalded his legs and hands nearly to the waist, but 'that proved sufficient to cause his death in the course of Taesday even- ing. It is a rare thing for any one who gets lain the brine, whether by accident or carelessness, to recover., Deceased leaves a family to suffer for his loss.

BAN 7V OF HOPE.—The Wesleyan Band of Hopl,(Hill Top Chapel), have had a service in which the chief actors were the maater of the Leftwich Workhouse, Mr. Howarth, and the workhouse children, whom he has taught tc sing and recite very nicely. They were assisted by Midi3Olive Brock, who became quite a favourite with the muting by ' her excellent rendering of '"['he Swiss Toy Girl,". in Char- acter; "The Silver Herrin," and" MY Baby." child- ren, among other songs, did well in " Whistling 'Tom," "The Farmer John," "The Three Little Pigs," and the "Burl esqne Band," Which was warmly greeted. . Seteral plece3 were well recited, but none created more amuse- ment than "Ten Somebodies." Afters very pleasant-hour and a half, votes of thanks to the performers brought the pleasant evening to a close.

A TRACTION ENGINE ON THE HIGHWTY.I-At the' New- ton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, George Carter, of Wigan, was summoned for allowing a locomotive engine to be on the highway between the hours prohibited in the bye- - laws of the county justices.—The defendant pleaded guilty. —P.C. Rigby deposed that on Tuesday, the 6th Feb.,,about ten mintites- to six, he saw a traction engine going along the high-road at Winwick and coming from - Cie direction of Warrington, going towards • Wigan. lie spoke to the defendant (who was in charge), and asked him if he knew be was contravening the byelaws. • He re- - replied that he could go any time during the night in the country if he carried lights. Witness told 'him he was-- wrong, and said he would have to be reperrted.-Lltihb de- fendant said he had nothing to say beyond the fad that he • had the working of the Act in his possession, and that was what he went by.—The Chairman : You seem to hate been led away by your Act. We will deal very-. leittently with you, and fine you 10s. and costs.

div.head: Xettelo to the editor.
div.p: Xettelo to the editor.
RUNCORN POLITICAL PARTIES.

Sir,—! had no sooner sent off my brief letter on the above subject last week, than I was infermed that in conse- quence of the death of Lord Egerton, the meeting to which I referred was postponed. It is, however, more than likely that we shall be involved in a severe struggle for the seat rendered vacant by the elevation of the senior member for Mid-Cheshire to the House of Lords. The Liberal senti- • ment in Runcorn is very strong, and if the other parts of • the division are only a little more favourable to the Liberal candidate than they were at the general election, we shall gain the seat, and save the constituency from the Tory dominance which has for so long blighted the political hope of Mid-Cheshire. The probaWe appointment of a Liberal lord-lieutenant for the county will doubtless give an impetus to Liberalism in Cheshire, cud is an indication of the ultimate overthrow of the Tory stronghold. This will, of course, be a work of time; our immediate task is to secure the seat just vacated. Mr. Latham's reiterated declarations on the absolute secrecy of the ballot must surely have had a good effect on the minds of those timid voters who, though they think right, vote wrong, through fear of the landlord finding out how they vote. It seems almost incredible that such obtuseness should still exist in the bucolic mind; and though the Conservative leaders may deny that there is anything in it, they know full well that their hope lies in this direction. From the day when the farming classes are delivered from the political bondage which has oppressed them we may date the downfall of that power which is so inimical to the best interests of the people, viz., Toryism. I am not sorry that there is a prospect of an election.contest in this division; for nothing educates public opinion so well as the numerous meetings which are the necessary ac- companiments of an election. Liberalism has nothing to Jose, and everything to gain from a free and full discussion .of all the questions that are before the public. The Runcorn Liberals are ready and eager for the fray, and it is only fair to admit that the Conservatives of the town, with a most energetic secretary and numerous assistants, together with the church clergy and nearly every magistrate on the bench, will make a respectable show, and furnish foemen worthy of the Liberal steel. I hope the Liberal party throughout the division will fight shoulder to shoulder with determination and zeal, and then we may see our tried and trusted friend, G. W. Latham, triumphantly returned as member for Mid-Cheshire.—Yours, RADIC.th. February 26th, 1583.

REPRESENTATION OF MID- CHESHIRE. THE SELECTION OF CANDIDATES. M Theid .0 h pe sohl ii trice ao la npoaortt i be i es a ono ot shee d of Parliamentary dilatoriness idol sr- ei sgi ao tnd ot of setting in motion the electoral machinery for the purpose of filling up the vacancy caused by Lord Egerton 's death and the consequent removal of the sitting member, the on. Wilbraham Enerton, to the Upper House. Although it was announced that no steps were to be taken until ..ter the funeral, which took place on Tuesday, thr.re must have been active preparations going on from the moment it was known that a contest was imminent. Both the can- didates were ready, and early on Tuesday afternoon their addresses were issued. The Liberal representative, Mr. Geenge William Latham, who has twice previously con- 'tested the di7ision, and on the last occasion, in 1880, came very near the second Conservative member, Mr. Piers E. Warburton, was selected some time ago as the champion of his party, and he has done much since that time by frequent appearances and public utterances to strengthen the bond of sympathy be- tween himself and the large proportion of voters who gave him their suffrages at the general election. In the Conser- vative camp the important question of a representative man was not so satisfactorily arranged. It was not to be expected that the political domination which the Egertons have so long enjoyed over a large partion of the county would be allowed to slip out of the -family, and according to reliable statements it was the wish of the late Lord Egerton that his second son, the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton, should take the place of his elder brother when the inevitable change occ-arred. To this natural request the Conservative land- owners and gentry in Mid-Cheshire have quite as naturally acceded. -Immediately the ceremonial at Restherne Church had concluded the assembled leaders of the party hastened to Knutsford Town Hall, where they formally adopted as their candidate the Hon. Alan Egerton. His election ad- dress" which was placed in the hands of his supporters with- -1 cut any further delay, is a declaration of political faith such las was to be expected from a gentleman of his family and training. Though admitting that he has nut been constantly resident in the county, he adds:—" I am not unknown to many of the electors, and the training I have had as a repre- sentative on the Metropolitan Board of Works has, I trust, -fitted me for the political career upon which I am anxious !to enter." He further says:—" lam a consistent Conserva- tive, and shall uphold the institutions of Church and State," ' but follows by a declaration that he "will not oppose such progress as may be required to adapt our existing constitu- tion to the requirements of the age." A disposition to con- cede to the tenant farmer that which all parties of late years agree in thinking is but bare justice namely, compensation for unexhausted improvements—is shown by the :candidate, who expresses himself as in favour of immediate legislation securing that benefit to the farmer, and he makes a further bid for the agricultural vote in supporting the proposal to afford relief to the agricultural interest by obtaining contributions to- wards the local rates from those classes of property which are now exempted. Mr. Egerton records his disapproval of the Government's policy in Ireland during the last three years, but gives his adhesion to Lord Spencer's present policy, and is opposed to all further concessions tending to the disintegration of the empire. The Conservative party appear to be confident of the result of the contest, as they claim to have largely increased their strength at recent di- visions. In spite of this confidence, however, a diligent canvass is being made, and the battle will be fought as though the initial advantages which attend the Conserva- tive candidate had no existence. Amongst the opposite party the unity and enthusiasm are, if anything, greater. Mr. Latham, whose gallant attacks on the Egerton strong- hold have won him many earnest supporters, is now enter- ing upon the contest with more favourable omens than have " sat upon his banners" on any previous occasion. His party also claim to have gained by careful attention to the register many votes that would extinguish the unfavourable majority in 1880, and certainly, from the arrangements now made, no effort will be spared to awaken all °Liberal voters in the division to a sense of their duty in the present struggle. A largely attended meeting of his supporters was held last evening at the Reform Club, Altrincham, at which Sir Joseph C. Lee presided. It was unanimously and en- thusiastically resolved to contest the seat, and the choice of the "Four Hundred," which had fallen on Mr. Latham, was endorsed amidst cheers. The candidate then entered the meeting, and was loudly applauded. His election address, which had been published during the day, states that he is prepared to give a "general and independent support" to the present Government. The programme for the session, as announced in the Queen's Speech, promised much useful legislation. The principles of local and municipal government were to be settled, elections were to be made less expensive and more pure, and a bill to provide compensation for unexhausted improvements by the tenant farmers was to be introduced. "I am convinced," he says, "that no bill on this subject will be adequate which does not contain provisions that no tenant shall leave his farm without full payment for what lie has expended in raising its letting value, and which he has not got back, that no sitting tenant shall have his rent raised upon his own improvements, and that theme shall be full freedom of sale and culture. I would most earnestly support a bill containing these provisions, and feel sure they may be carried out without infringing the rights of owners of the soil. I belies e also that the pre- sent law of agricultural distraint is indefensible, and is as injurious to the tradesman as it is oppressive to the occupier." Mr. Latham refers to the Municipal and County Govern- ment Bills, and expresses his hope that there may be power given by those measures to the representatives of the rate- payers to deal with the question of licenses. He is in favour of the assimilation of the franchises, supports the Govern- ment policy in Ireland, and points with pleasure to the equalisation of the salt duties in India, which allows im- ported salt to compete on fair terms with the native product. In conclusion, Mr. Latham appeals, as a thirty years' resident in Cheshire and as one who has hitherto tried to serve his fellow-men, for the suffrages of the electors. The willing services of several well-known members of Parliament, including the Hon. E. Lyulph Stanley (Oldham), Mr. W. C. Borlase (East Cornwall), Mr. Henry Broadhurst (Stoke-on-Trent), and Mr. James Howard (Bed- fordshire), have been enlisted in Mr. Lathani's behalf, and it is expected that these gentlemen will speak at one or other of the numerous meetings to be held during the cam- paign. Nothing will be left undone on the part of the Cheshire Liberals to place Mr. Latham at the head of the poll. On and all are working hard to secure this result, believing that the return of Mr. Latham for Mid-Cheshire would not only announce the overthrow of the system by which an important constituency has been long field as a family appanage, but would also add to the Liberal majority in the House of Commons, a well-qualified exponent of agricultural claims, and a member who would represent, not alone the land-owing class, but the whole of the influential community by whom he had been elected. The 3fark Lane Express says :—The farmers of Mid- Cheshire will have an opportunity of sending to Parliament one of the best of candidates for an agricultural constitu- ency, now that there is to be an election to supply the vacancy caused by the succession of Mr. Egerton. M.P., to his just-deceased father's peerage. It has been understood timat Mr. G. W. Latham would come forward once more on the first opportunity, and it is now announced that he will do so after Lord Egerton's funeral. Mr. Latham, although a landlord, is an advanced agricultural reformer, and a vice- president of the Farmers' Alliance. He has long been known in Cheshire and the neighbouring counties as a staunch advocate of tenant-right and tenant-farmers inter- est%generally, and there is every reason to expect that the farmers of his own division will rally round him and retnrn him by a considerable majority.

LANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIETY. —The usual monthly meeting was held on Monday evening, in the Free Library, the president (Mr. S. J. Capper) occu- pying the chair. Miss H. Johnson, and Messrs. E. Nelson and G. T. Shaw were elected members of the society.—The President, in the course of a short address, referred to the death of one of the oldest members of the society—the late Mr. Benjamin Cooke, of Southport, and he gave a short resum6 of his life as an entomologist.—The hon. secretary (Dr. John W. Ellis) read a paper entitled " Passive means of defence in insects," in which he briefly noted a number of instances of protective resemblances in various orders of insects, and afterwards alluded to cases of so-called" mimi- cry " in lepidoptera.—The proceedings terminated with the usual cenversazione, during which Mr. R. Brown exhibited a specimen of Nyssia Zonaria which had remained about twenty months in the pupa state, and Mr. J. Wall exhibited scales of lepidoptera under the microscope.

div.head: PREVIOUS ELECTIONS IN MID-CHESHIRE.
div.p: PREVIOUS ELECTIONS IN MID-CHESHIRE.

In glancing over the political history of the county since it was divided by the first Reform Act, the predominant in- fluence of three families is remarkably apparent. The changes are rung upon the names of Egerton, Tollemache, and Legh with singular regularity. In the wave of Liberal enthusiasm which succeeded the passing of the Reform Bill, the Right Hon. E. J. Stanley afterwards raised to the peerage as Baron Eddisbury, headed the poll in North Cheshire, the late Lord Egerton being next, while Mr. J. R. D. Tollemache, the second Conservative candidate was de- feated. The seat thus secured ty Mr. William Tatton Egerton, was retained by him against all corners until his elevation to the peerage by the late Lord Derby, more than a quarter of a century later, Mr. Egerton being accompanied to the Lords, by Sir Charles Morgati, as Lord Tredegar, for good service rendered to the Conservative party i-i Mon- mouthshire, and by Sir John Yarde-Bulleras Lord Churston. for having proved a tower of strength to the Tory party in South Devon, where he had driven Lord John Russell from his seat many years before. The representation of North Cheshire was divided between Mr. E. J. Stanley and Mr. Tatton Egerton until the general election of 1841, when, amid the Conservative reaction, Mr. George Cornwall Leg!' came in as a second Conservative, and Mr. Stanley lost his seat, which, however, he regained without opposition in 1817. In the following year he received a peerage from Lord John Russell, and Mr. Legh was elected for the seat thus vacated, beating Mr. Francis Astley by more than 600 votes. From that time the Conservatives had a monopoly of the representation, the names of Egerton and Legh regu- larly appearing in the returns. Lord Egerton of Talton was succeeded by his son, and when the Reform Act of 1867 split the county into three divisions, the northern disappeared politically, and its two members went to the mid-division, in which the present vacancy occurs. The first election in it was in November, 1868, when the hon. J. B. L. Warren fought a gallant but losing battle in the Liberal interests, not breaking the continuity of Messrs. Egerton and Legh. In March, 1872, Mr. George Cornwall Legh died, and a contest ensued, in which the conservatives brought out Colonel Egerton Legb, who defeated Mr. G. W. Latham by 1,500 votes. In 1874, when Mr. Disraeli came into power as the result of the dissolution, the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton and Col. Egerton Legh were returned for Mid-Cheshire without opposition; and in July, 1876, on the decease of the latter, Mr. Piers Egerton was elected unopposed. At the last general election: however, there was a very severe contest, , each party running two candidates, with this result—Eger- ton, 3,868; Warburton, 3,700; Latham, 3374. Armitage, 3,247. It will be seen that between Mr. Warburton and Mr. Latham there was a difference of only 320 votes. Mr. Latham now pluckily comes forward for the third time, and will receive the united support of his party in his en- deavours to liberate the division from the domination of one great county family. While the Egertons and.Leghs thus figured so conspicuously in North and Mid-Cheshire, Egerton and Tollemache were' long the names of the two

div.head: EAAMINEPt., sAitithAy, MARCH 3, 1883.
div.p: THE EAAMINEPt., sAitithAy, MARCH 3, 1883.

members for the south and west. It is true that, amid great Liberal wave of 1832, Sir Philip Egerton was r-,/etta in South Cheshire, but he obtained a seat for that alvision in 1835, and held it until his death, two yeArs AgN h 1841 he was joined- by the present 149!-d ollerauhe, 'who "riz-1 ceeded in ousting Mr. George W;iorahuaarl ,30 impreg- nable was the Tory p°3lt.Lon regarded in south Cheshire, that Sir Philip T...gerton and Mr. Tollemache were not mo.lesttd• in February, 1872, whei tile latter retired after 11:Ac1ing the seat without challenge more than 30 years, his eldest son took undisputed posse.ssion of it; and in 1874, Sir Philip Egerton mu? Mr. Tollemache enjoyed the luxury of an 'unopposed return. In 1876, Mr. Disraeli paid the same debt to Mr. John Tollemache for what he had done in South Cheshire as Lord Der's, ba'd to Mr. William Tatton Egerton for his services in ',he northern division and created him a peer. In 1880, for the first time during nearly 40 years, a contest took place in West (formerly South) Cheshire, Sir Philip Egerton and Mr. W. F. Tollemache beating Major Corn- wallis West and Mr. Charles Crompton. Meanwhile, with the disappearance of the northern division of Cheshire, the eastera had been created by the measure of 1868, which gave 25 additional members to Tory counties. It proved very safe to allow two extra seats to Cheshire. We have already seen that at the first election under that act the mid- division returned the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton and Mr. George Cornrall Legh, and' the western division sent in I Sir Philip Egerton and Mr. John Tollemache. The eastern division came to the conclusion that it had better secure as muck uniformity as possible in the representation of the county by electing Mr. E. C. Egerton and Mr. Legb. Thus an Egerton was conveniently useful for each of the three divisions, and a Legh lot two. This was very good for the familia immediately concerned, but it is hoped that a time has come when the influence so lung exercised by two of three great houses over a whole county can be materially reduced. Their day has been a long one, and two out of the three have had peerages as the reward of their efforts in the Tory cause. An Egerton has now for the time dis- appeared, and, by a vigorous and united endeavour in sup- port of Mr. Latham, the Liberals of Mid-Cheshire will pro- bably take care that one Egerton this time is not succeeded by another.
MR. LATHAM AT MIDDLEVVICH.

A meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Latham was held on Thursday afternoon at the Town Hall, Middle- wich. There was a good attendance. The chair was occu- pied by the Rev. F. Minton, vicar of the parish, and there were also on the platform Mr. Latham Mr. W. C. Borlase, M.P., Mr. James Tomkinson, Mr. V. Milne, and other gentlemen. After a few remarks from the chairman, Mr. LATHAM, who was very cordially received, said that in his belief there was much to be done in Parliament in the way of social reform as in other political work. Vice and misery and crime in this country all wanted lessening by all our exertions, and though he believed it to be impossible to make man virtuous by Act of Parliament, yet he was quite certain that by the enactment of wise laws and the repeal of bad laws we might do much to give scope to the efforts of individuals toward the en- couragement of virtue and the repression of crime. (Hear, hear.) Referring to a letter he bad received that morning, asking him to say "yes or no," whether he would vote for his opponent, Mr. Alan de Tatton Egerton, he said that he knew that on a previous occasion letters of that kind were followed on many estates by a visit from the land agent, and if the farmer scrupled to write the agent wrote in the "yes" where he thought the farmer should. He (Mr. Latham) told the farmers that they had the ballot now, and the people ought to reverence the law in the spirit as well as in the letter. He did not think it was very becom- ing for gentlemen in the position of Mr. Egerton to try so to violate the Act which was passed giving them that privi- lege. (Hear, hear.) Criticising the address of Mr. Egerton, he said that with regard to compensation to farmers, no bill on that subject would be adequate that did not contain a provision that no tenant should leave his farm without full payment for what he • had expended, and which he had not got back, and that no tenant should have his rent raised for his own improvements, as well as giving full freedom of sale and culture. While declaring himself a thorough Liberal, he had to say that if the Government fell short of its professions in regard to agricultural reform, and did not help the farmer, he would oppose the Government himself. But they in the county constituencies would never get a lowered franchise from the Conservatives, or if they got it, it would be with a grudging hand. Before the close of the present Parliament the Government would bring in a bill to make the county franchise the same as that of the boroughs, and to those who possessed the franchise he ap- pealed that they should not be so selfish as to refuse it to their brethren who did not. (Cheers.) Mr. Tnomes Humus proposed a resolution approving of the candidature of Mr. Latham, and pledging the meeting to use all legitimate means to secure his return. Mr. JOSEPH MILLINGTON, a tenant farmer, seconded the resolution, observing that he hoped that tenant farmers of Mid• Cheshire would come out and exercise their rights. They had no better friend in the division than Mr. Latham. (Applause.) Mr. BORLASE, M.P, supported the resolution. He said what the farmer really wanted was to be placed exactly on the same level with the manufacturer, and to be able to go to his banker on the same conditions and with the same credit that another man can do. While an atom of the law of distress remained it was impossible that he could do so. (Hear, bear.) The farmer did not wish to be the only man who was called apon to speculate upon another man's good intentions or to trust to another man's honour. First of all, then, they must get rid of the law of distress; in the second place, the tenant must be able to expend his money en his holding in the manner in which be thought best, and in the third place his rent must not be inequitably raised upon improvements which he had made.
- Mr. Jes. Tommisow and Mr. Wm. MILNE supported the resolution, which was unanimously carried.
MR. LATHAM AT WINSFORD.

A largely attended meeting was held on Thursday even- ing at the Town Hall Winsford, in support of Mr. Latham's candidature. The chair was taken by Mr. Joseph Slater. There were also on the platform the Rev. Symonds, the Rev. C. Reader, Mr. R. Stubbs, Mr. T. Holland, and Mr. J. W. Cooke.

Mr. LATHAN said that whatever advantages—and he dared say they were considerable—that his opponent might possess over him of rank and fortune, he, at all events, had the advantage that the electors knew him, and he knew them. He had been a resident in Mid-Cheshire now for more than 30 years, and he claimed that during that time he must have acquired a knowledge of the wants of the , place in which he lived. (Hear.) He did not believe that his opponent, although he had been blessed by election to the Metropolitan Board of Works, could be quite so conver- sant with the internal economy of the county of Chester as one who for nearly thirty years had acted as a magis- trate, and for more than thirty years had been a landlord in the county. (Cheers.) Another advantage he claimed to have was that his address to the constituency meant something, while Mr. Egerton's meant nothing at all. (Cheers.) If they elected the man who wrote the latter they might elect a very honest fellow and a perfect gentleman, but they would not elect one who knew in the smallest de- gree anything about politics. He was convinced that the writer of that document was simply a politician, because he was told he was to he a member of Parliament, and not, as he (Mr. Latham) was a candidate, because he was a poli- tician. Was Mr. Egerton, if elected, going to follow Sir Stafford Northcote, or would he be content to belong to the Fourth party? It seemed to him absurd for anybody to talk of belonging to the Conservative party, for it had gone. (Hear, hear.) It was non-exlstent at the present moment. (Cheers.) Was Mr. Egerton in favour of the extension of the franchise to the counties and the redistribution of seats? It was only a truism to say that the county franchise must be assimilated to that of the boroughs. When the men of War- rington,the sailors of Liverpool,and the ironworkers atSaltney had votes he could not see why they should be denied to , the saltwerkers of Winsford. (Cheers.) The grievances of the farmers which the Government wished to remedy was not merely a farmer's or a landlord's question, but affected the whole of the population of the country, inasmuch as the land should be made to produce as much as it could, and the less security there was for the farmer's capital the less the land would be cultivated and the less it would pro- duce. He wished to congratulate those employed in the salt trade of that district on the fact that the Government had culled out the doctrines of free trade by equalising the salt duties in India. Although the good effects to be ex- pected from that measure had not vet been felt, they might look forward to surmounting the difficulties which stood in the way through the influence of the ring of native salt sellers in that country. (Hear, hear.) Mr. REUBEN STUBBS moved a resolution declaring that Mr. Latham was a fit and proper person to represent that constituency in Parliament. Mr. T. HOLLAND, a farmer, seconded the resolution. He said that Mr. Latham would not be a " dummy " in the House of Commons. They had had enough of these "dum- mies" in past years. (Laughter.) That large county sent six members to Parliament, and they scarcely ever read a speech of their members out of Cheshire. (Laughter.) It was said there was one who was in Parliament for 40 years, and only Once spoke, and then he said, "Draw that cur- tain." (Much laughter.) He asked them to return a man on this occasion who would do • something for them, and he was sure they had such a man in Mr. Latham. (Cheers.) Mr. BORLASE, M.P., also supported the resolution. The lan4 laws of this country, he said, wanted unmaking. We must not legislate for the landlord, for Heaven knew he had had enough done for him already—(cheers); nor for the tenant, though he required it enough; nor for the labourer, although he had been ground down enough by these very laws; nor even for the consumer; but for the soil itself, that each individual might take out of it that which God had provided for all. (Cheers.) Mr. JAS. TOMBINSON also supported the resolution, which was carried with only one dissentient. The proceedings terminated with thanks to the chairman for presiding.
