eision for a num- ber of elections since 1863. In 1868 some of them would remember that Mr. Warren was put forward by the Liberals as the candidate for their suffrages, and the result of that election was as follows :—For Egerton 3,171 votes, Legh 3,057, Warren 2,482. (Cheers.) For a long time previous to that contest the Liberals had done very little in the county, and the consequence was that Mr. Warren had 575 fewer votes than Mr. Legh, the lowest of the Conservative candidates. At that election 5,551 persons voted out of 7,158 voters who were on the register, so that 1,607 voters did not record their votes. Then they came to 1872. In that year there was a contest. Mr. Latham came forward as the Liberal candidate and Mr. Legh as the Tory candi- date. The number of votes polled for the latter was 3,508, and for Mr. Latham 2,118, or 1,490 fewer than Mr. Legh, so that they would see they polled considerably fewer 'votes than in 1868. He might tell them that nothing whatever was done to the register during those years. Liberalism was allowed to take its own course. The Tories had always been busy on the register, putting on all those of their own side. Of course the great aim of the Tory party had ever been to keep off the register the masses of the people. But an effort had been made by the Liberal party, and he believed a measure would be carried through Parliament by the present Government to give a similar vote to the men in the counties as was now enjoyed by the men in the boroughs. (Loud cheers.) There was no reason why the intelligent ratepayers of a town like Runcorn should be deprived of the franchise. (Hear, hear.) They had to pay rates and taxes—all the charges that were imposed upon large ratepayers, with few exceptions, were put upon every householder. Then if he was taxed and rated why ought he not to have a vote for a member for Parliament,so that he might be represented in the legislature of the country. (Cheers.) It was very difficult to get intelligent reasons from the other side as to why they stood so much against the masses having political power. Of course they said at times that the masses were too ignorant to exercise the fran- chise, and, therefore ought not to ha granted the privilege of voting, but it seemed to him—he did not know whether he was right or wrong—tbat if working men were intelligent enough to pay rates and taxes to support the national ex- penditure, he certainly ought to be intelligent enough to vote for a member of Parliament. (Loud cheers.) In 1868 there were 1,607 voters who did not record their votes, and it was a remarkable fact that in 1872, 1,874 persons ab- stained from voting. At the general election of 1874 there was no contest in Mid-Cheshire, and in 1876 on the decease of Colonel Egerton Leigh, Mr. Piers Warburton was returned without a contest. In 1880 there was a contest in this division. Egerton had 3,868 votes recorded for him. Warburton, 3,700, Latham, 3,374, and Armitage, 3,247. He wished to record the very great change which had taken place in Mid-Cheshire between 1872, when Latham was 1,490 votes below the other candi- date and 1880, when that majority had been reduced to 326. (Loud cheers.) In the latter year 1,033 persons abstained from voting, whilst at the previous election 1,874 did not vote. It would thus appear that for some reason or other, a very large proportion of those who had been put upon the register and had abstained from voting in previous years, gave their suffrages' in to the Liberal candidate in 1880. (Cheers.) What was their position to-day? Had they any rea- son to expect any better result in 1883 to the result in 1880? He might safely say that from 1872 to 1880 the Liberals had done very little to the register; hut from 1880 to the present time the register had been in a very satisfactory position. (Loud cheers.) What he meant by that was that they had endeavoured to put on the register those persons that ought to be on. It was considered that the register was so satisfactory as to give them a large majority at the com- ing contest. (Cheers.) He hoped, amongst other measures to be brought forward by the Government, would be one that would remove the great difficulty that existed in attending to the register. He thought it was a disgrace to a nation like this, after the experience of years, there should be any necessity for any person whatever to attend to the register, because he took it that when they got the assimilation of the borough and county franchise every householder would be put upon the register, and a great deal of the difficulty and trouble in refer- ence to this question would be removed. (Cheers.) They had every reason to expect that if they entered into this matter as they ought to do, they would be able to re- turn a Liberal member of Parliament for Mid-Cheshire. (Loud cheers.) There were strong reasons why they ought to return a man like Mr. Latham,—(cheers)—and there were as strong reasons why a person like Alan Egerton ought not to be returned. (Cheers.) At present, at all events, they did not object to the House of Lords. It was a chamber where the aristocracy was represented, and where they had always looked after their own interests—(laughter and cheers)—at the expense of the masses of the people. Nearly all the laws had been framed for their benefit, and whilst they did not now say that that chamber ought to be abolished, they looked upon it as a crime for English work- men of whatever colour, whether Liberal or Tory, to bring the sons of the aristocracy into the House that ought to be representative of the people. (Loud cheers.) If they took the member who had just been transferred from one house to the other, he had only been advocating that protection for his class in the Lower House, which he was now going to protect to the best of his ability in the Upper House. And therefore he (Mr. Shaw) thought it was to the interest of both parties—Liberal and Conservative workingmen at all events—not to send the class of men like Alan Egerton to the House of Commons. (Hear, bear, and loud cheers.) If he (Mr. Shaw) were a Tory he should prefer to vote for a commercial man than for the son of a peer, simply because a commercial man in the House of Commons would be able to understand questions affecting the benefit of the masses in commercial matters, and he should expect that they would be very much better from appear- ance than they would be from the son of an aristocrat. (Cheers.) When they looked at the present constitution of the House. they saw that they had a great many of these gentlemen there whose sole interest it was to keep things as they were—almost any question might be discussed in the House of Commons if its aim was to keep things just where they were. There were many questions that were pressing to the fore-front which could not be delayed much longer, and to some of these Mr. Latham re- ferred in his address, which was decided upon on the pre- vious night, and accepted by the Liberals of the division. Mr. Shaw concluded by reading Mr. Latham's address, the more telling parts of which were loudly cheered. Mr. J. R. FRITH was called upon to move the first reso- lution. He said he wished he could say brother electors to all of them, because he saw so many present who he believed ought to have a voice in the election of a member for Par- liament. (Loud cheers.) They were about to engage in a strong contest, wben, no doubt, feeling would run high— when they would have to meet with difficulties, and, per- haps, some hard words—but whilet there was no one worked harder, or threw themselves more heartily into work of this kind, he could safely say that he had never made a political enemy. (Cheers.) He believed that everyone who worked, either for the Liberal or the Conservative , cause, could work heartily without making enemies, and that night he would say, "gentlemen, whatever you do, fight your hardest, do your best, and don't make enemies." (Cheers.) The man who would make an enemy of them because they expressed an opinion—he did not call him a man. A man was a being who thought, spoke, and acted for himself; if he allowed another to do these things for him he was no man. (Cheers.) It was the birth- right of every Englishman to use that power which Parliament bad put into his hands, and if he threw it away he was throwing away his birthright. He (Mr. Frith) yielded to men's opinions in some things, but he would never allow any man to influence him in how he should vote for a mem- ber of Parliament. He first acquired that right through being a freeman of the borough in which he resided. His father was a freeman before him, and he inherited the privi- lege from him, and he looked upon it as a birthright. He felt that day that having a voice in the election of a mem- ber for Parliament he ought to conscientiously vote for the beat man—for the man that would do the best for the greatest number. (Cheers.) They had not to vote for a man because they thought he would help him as an individual. They must vote for a man who would help the majority. The majority was to be considered, not the minority. Let them look to the great majority of their fellow creatures and let them try to do the best they could for them. But it was not his intention to speak at all that night, and he was rather surprised that he had been called upon to address them first. He felt that they ought not to say much that night, but in a contest of this kind he thought it was neces- sary to make these remarks about not manifesting personal feeling to those they came in contact with. In every election, both for School Boards and Commissioners, he had had to work in the midst of Tories. There were a great many Tories whom he respected, and who were intimate friends of his, perhaps the best friends he had, and he worked heartily with them—cracked some splendid jokes with them—and when they had either won or lost they have been good friends. That was his advice to them that night. (Cheers.) He Jett that this was a question of (mlineacrh,. he(affr.e)ar, hear.)lt w s Don'tof often said drktihnagt aLnidbenraolts let that be said of Wem during that election. The great thing was to work, and he was glad to find that some had talking. too already set to work. Many present were ready and waiting to be put into harness, and to go forth and work. The resolution which had been into his hands was as follows : "That the best efforts of all persons present shall be put forth to secure the return of Mr. G. W. Latham." He did

not know who had drawn up this resolution, but he con- gratuled him upon his foresight. The resolution, they would notice, said " all pereons present," not the voters present. No. (Cheers.) Those who were expecting to be voters ; (cheers)—those who were voters, and those that were look- ing forward to enjoy that privilege, and if they worked at this election and did their best to secure the return of Mr. Latham, they would only be hastening the time when they would have a vote given to them. He believed the non- electors in any constituency very often did more work than the electors themselves, because there were so many in the counties who were non-electors, and they int uenced a great many electors. One man said to another "I should advise you to vote for Mr. Latham simply because you are voting for a true Liberal, and if you assist in dwelling the majority of that great and noble man IV. E. Gladstone— (prolonged cheering)—you are only hastening the time when I, as a non-elector, shall become an elector, because I believe that Mr. Gladstone, before the expiration of the present Pa-, liament, will pass a Bill to assimilate the borough mi'd county franchise." Mr. Frith again urged those pre.-jeut to work—to try their utmost in this election to secure, the re- turn of Mr. Latham, because he was a tried ne,", a good man. He was not an ornamental man who 'Would go before them with an eye-glass on, saying " Ham, (Loud laughter.) He was a true born and a. etraightforward Eng- lishman, who appeared what he w-as, and who would do his utmost for people in the Britis'Ta House of Commons He I spoke of him as being in. the House of Commons.. He believed he would be. Tie prospect of the election certainly pointed to the return -of Mr. G. W. Latham. (Cheers.) Mr. W. HANDLLY, who was cordially received, seconded the resolution with great pleasure. He would only advance two or three reasons why they should support the candida- ture of Mr. G. W. Latham. The first was, that the principle of fair play ought to rule in this election. Was it not a fact that it was something like 30 years since they had a Liberal representative for Mid-Cheshire? He thought they must all agree that both sides of opinion in any constituency ought atany rate to be represented after such a lengthened period, and they were not asking too much in asking all persons, whether they be Conservatives cr Liberals, to vote for, and assist in, returning to the House of Commons so good a man as Mr. Latham. Before coming to the meeting he read a speech by the Honourable Alan Egerton, and taking into account the sad and painful circumstances under which that speech was delivered, he must say that it spoke well for that gentleman. He made use of one sentence that they as Liberals could take encourage- ment from. It was this: "Man's first duty he owes to his country." The Liberal party, it was said, had done more for the country in the past 50 years than was done in tAe previous 100 years when it was under Conservative rule, and if .a man owed his first duty to his country he certainly owed a debt to the Liberal party; and the majority of that party ought to be increased as largely as possible. There was another reason why they should return Mr. Latham, and that was that within a very short period of time—certainly during the life of the present Parliament—there would a number of questions come up for discussion and settlement, prominent amongst which was the question of the formation of County Boards. Living in towns they might not perhaps see so much the necessity for County Boards as those did who lived in the country. They scarcely knew what was meant by by the formation of County Boards. But a close examination of the question showed that it affected those in the towns as much as it did those who lived in the rural districts, because it was a fact that nearly one-half of the amount that every ratepayer paid as poor rates was passed over to the county exchequer, with- out there being any control on the part of the ratepayers. Well, County Boards were meant to remedy this. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) As a member of the Board of Guardians it came before him in this way. Supposing the Guardians thought it necessary to demand a rate of something like 6d. in the pound, this would realise about £6,000 every half year. Between two and three thousand pounds had to be collected by the overseers of the various townships and passed over to the credit of the Union or Guar- dians' fund, and whenever the county authori- ties sent a precept for so much of the money, it had to be forthcoming and sent on to them. This was all very well or would be if, as according to the old English principle, taxation and representation went together. (Hear, hear.) The taxes of the country were drawn from the bulk of the people, and the bulk of the people sent, or ought to send members to Parliament. (Cheets.) In the case to which he was referring, the rate- payers had no control directly or indirectly over the expen- ditare of the money they provided. He did not wish to infer that the money was improperly spent, or that it would be more wisely spent by representatives of the ratepayers on County Boards, but he did say that so long as they had to contribute the money they ought to have a voice in its expenditure—(cheers)—and they ought to know how the money was spent. If they would examine the quarterly accounts given at the sessions, they would find that a large I amount of money was spent under the head of county busi- ness, and that was all they knew about it. And when be told them that although the Guardians of Runcern Union contributed about £6,000 a year to the county funds (a large proportion of which came from Run- corn), they only got during the year two balance sheets to show how that money was expended, they would see that there was something radically wrong in the administration of county business so far as representation was concerned. He thought it would be conceded on all hands that Mr. Latham understood the administration of county business as well, if not better, than any man in Cheshire. It must certainly be conceded that between Mr. Latham and Mr. A. Egerton there could scarcely be a comparison drawn. Mr. Latham, as one of the chairmen of Quarter Sessions, had had opportunities of gaining knowledge and experience in connection with county business second to none in the division. Now, that was one question and a very pressing question that would have to come before Parliament very shortly. Let them then do their best to secure the return of Mr. Latham. (Cheers.) He believed that if the election depended upon Runcorn Mr. Latham's election would be assured. (Cheers.) But that was no reason why they should not see that every voter in Runcorn on the Liberal side was brought to the poll. Let each in- dividual voter do as much as he could to help forward the candidature of Mr. Latham. He hoped that the election would be conducted with as good humour as they did last time, but at the same time let them put their shoulder to the wheel and fight manfully, and then he had no doubt that Mr. Latham would be the member. (Cheers.) Mr. S. C. BECKETT supported the motion, remarking that he was quite prepared to do what he could to secure the re- turn of Mr. Latham, than whose address he did not think a better could be issued. (Hear, hear.) There was one point in that address, with regard to the licensing laws, which struck him very forcibly, and with which he agreed. (Cheers.) He had no doubt that in the present Parliament a satisfactory bill dealing with that quesron would be passed, and then they would see better days than they did at the present time. (Cheers.) Mr. B. KNIVETON said there was one very good reaeon why every workman ought to heartily support the c indide- tore of Mr. Latharn—(hear, hear)—and that was on account of his advanced views on the Land Question. (Hear, hear.) The food question was of the greatest importance—he sup- posed those present found it to be so. (Laughter.) Was it not a fact that, if the Land Laws were improved, the land would be capable of yielding nearly 50 percent. more produce than it did now ? (Cheers.) The result of the vicious Land Laws which prevailed, which had been made by the great landowners of the country with a view to the protection of their own interest exclusively, was that the price of food was exceedingly high. They ought to send men to the House of Commons who would undo this class legislation —(hear, bear, and cheers)—and remove all unnecessary re- strictions from the land, allowing the farmer to set to work untrammelled, reaping from his land as much produce as he could. The people wanted cheap food—(cheers)--- for those who were engaged in commercial life must admit that the day of large profits had gone by. (Hear, hear.) He thought they would now have to face a period of small profits and quick returns— (laughter)—and that they would never see that period of high wages that obtained some years ago. (Hear, bear.) But if they could get an improvement in the Land Laws food would be cheaper, and the working people would be in just as good a position. (Hear, hear.) What was the use of having exceedingly high gages, if the price of every- thing they had to purchase was correspondingly high ? Let the Land Laws be altered, give the farmer an incentive to cultivate his farm to the utmost, and there would be a reduc- tion of 20 to 25 per cent, in food. (Cheers.) There was not a man in Cheshire—he was going to say England—who -understood the Land Laws better than Mr. Latham. (Cheers.) He bad a perfect grasp of the subject, and it was men of such a character that they wanted in Parliament. What did they want with a lot of young earls and lords? They wanted practical men—(cheers)—men that knew what the dangers and difficulties of life were, and that knew how to find out an evil and remove it. Those men were legislators who endeavoured to promole the welfare and happiness of as many as they possibly could, and therefore every man who wanted some- thing to 'eat good and cheap ought to support Mr. Latham (Loud cheers.) The day of class legis- lation was doomed. Workingmen were not now content. to be oppressed like they were 20 or 50 years ago. Everything was then done for the benefit of the parson and squire, but those days were over now. (Cheers.) .Every man felt that he was a man—(hear, hear)—and that., inasmuch as he con- tributed to the expenditure of the nation, he ought to have a voice in its representation. (Cheers.) Those who read the history of Conservatism, knew .that they had always legislated for classes—for parsons, bishops, and landowners, colonels and generals, and all that class—(laughter)—while the great majority had been left to get .along as best they could. Mr. Kniveton concluded by urging those present to use every effort to return Mr. Latham. The motion was then put and carried unanimously. Mr. LEAK, the secretary, announced that a meeting would be held on Tuesday evening, when Mr. Latham and several members of Parliament would address the electors. The meeting then terminated. (Continued on page 8.)

GOOD TEMPLARS' MEETING.—The members of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars held their usual weekly meeting on Monday evening last, when there was a pretty fair attendance. Brother G. E. Warburton, W.C.T., presided. At the close of the lodge business an interesting and profitable entertainment was held. Songs were given by Sisters Allison, Whitty, Brothers A. Allison, Henry War- burton, and Elliott, and a duet by Sisters Whitty and Har- riman. Recitations were given by Brothers John Warburton and John Muggleton, and Sister M. Clark. Brother E. Newman gave a reading. The proceedines were of. a very pleasant character, and concluded about half-past nine.

div.head: IS THE BALLOT SECRET?
div.p: IS THE BALLOT SECRET?

It takes a long time as a rule before people realise the full benefits conferred upon the nation by an Act of Parliament —such as the Ballot Act of 1872. This act was intended, among other things, to prevent the landlords or their agents or stewards from forcing their tenants to vote for their can- didate at any election; and tenant farmers should under- stand that the way they vote—the candidate they vote for —is not and cannot be known to their landlord or his agent or steward unless the tenant himself lets out the secret. Let us suppose that a steward or agent has asked a tenant farmer for his vote, and pressed him to pledge himself to vote for a certain candidate. When that tenant farmer goes into the polling place he can vote for whom he pleases without its being known to any one but himself. He receives a ballot paper from the presiding officer in the polling station, it is stamped with the official mark, the voter takes it to the secret compartment, Makes a cross against the name of the candidate he intends to vote for, folds the paper up so as only to show the official stamp on the back of the paper to the pre3iding officer, and puts it in the ballot box. When the papers are taken out of the boxes to be counted, the papers from Altriiacham, Sandbach, Con- gliaton, Northwich, and other placas are mixed together, and no person engaged as a counter or in any other capacity can tell where any paper comes from, much less can he tell whose it is, as it has only a X upon it. In this election every voter should remember this. The people should have complete confidence that when they are voting they are doing their own business in their own way, and that the laws of this country protect them in so doing. They should remember that any attempt to force them by threats of any kind, by agents or stewards, are illegal and punishable by imprisonment. In Mid-Cheshire election the tenant farmers can return Mr. Latham, who will advocate their cause on every occasion. They can have tie better advocate. He knows why they are suffering; he knows the remedy. He will support an Agricultural Holdings Act without a per- missive clause by which every landlord can contract himself out of it, which will give the tenant full value for his in- vestments in the soil he tills, just compensation for unexhausted improvements, and protect him with a business like lease. The Government Mr. Latham will support have already given to the tenant farmers the Ground Game Act, and they have repealed the malt tax, which the Tory party talked about for years and never touched. The present Government will give to agriculturists every consideration they can wish, and will probably establish a Ministry of Agriculture at no distant date. Every improvement in agriculture gives better employment to the labourer and more comforts for his family; and the working men of Mid-Cheshire should think of these things and reason them out, and they will see that their best friends are the Liberal party, and that in this contest they are helping one another, and speeding the day when every labourer will hay.e a vote, by supporting Mr. G. W. Latham, who is in every way eminently fitted to represent Mid-Cheshire in Parliament. And let every elector remember that, however he votes, the ballot is secret,, and protects him in giving his vote.

div.head: MR. G. W. LATHAM AT CONGLETON.
div.p: MR. G. W. LATHAM AT CONGLETON.

A meeting of the electors of the Congleton polling dis- tricts, in support of the candidature of Mr. G. W. Latham, the Liberal candidate, was held in the Town Hall, Congle- ton, on Wednesday night. Mr. John Latham (Congleton) occupied the chair. There were also on the platform Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., Mr. J. N. Peake Mr. J. 0. Nicholson, Mr. W. Milne, Mr. D. Duncan, and others. After a few remarks from the Chairman,

g Mr. LATHAM said he could not allow that opportunity to pass without expressing his regret at the death of Lord Egerton. (Hear, hear.) He had known him ever since his residence in the county, and he had always been treated by him with courtesy and kindness. Of course they differed on many political topics, and he looked at them in a dif- ferent light to that in which Lord Egerton Woke,' at them, but he never knew a man more fearless than Lord Egerton in expressing his opinions. (Hear, heat.) Lord Egerton was the most fearless man he ever saw. (Cheers.) He was thoroughly conversant with the business of the county, aria by his death he believed they had lost a most useful and gentlemanly nobleman. (Cheers.) And let him also say of their late member, the Hon. .Wilbraham (now Lord) Egerton, that however much he differed with him in poli- tics he was quite certain that he was always thoroughly conscientious, and his attention to his duties in the House of Commons constant and assiduous—(hear, hear)—and he did not think they could ask more from any one who was their member. But good as were the Egertons—much as he esteemed the late lord and the present lord—it was pos- sible they might have a little too much of a good thing. (Laughter.) The present . was not a fight against Egertons, but a fight for principles. The Egertons had always upheld Tory principles, and there were scores of Tories in the House now who, though not so outspoken as the Hon. Jas. Lowther, were ready to go back to the days of protection. The Hon. James Lowther bad asked for protection, and there were scores of members of the House of Commons who would, if they possibly could, bring us back to the days of protection, and he was almost going to say to the days of the Inquisition awl the Star Chamber. He left it to the constituency, with thorough confidence, to decide which was the hest policy for them—the policy of protec- tion and retrogression or the policy which set up their mills and workshops. The Tories bad advocated protection as best for the interests of agriculture, but he was of contrary opinion. The policy of retrogression must die out. (Hear, hear.) The policy of the present Government was the best policy for this country. It was the best because it was the most righteous. He asked them what Government before this, which had put false shame on one side, and dared, because it required an act of daring, knowing what the character of the English nation was, to withdraw its forces from Afghan- istan and to make peace in the transvaal, and would be willing, after occupying Egypt, to give it up again as it in- tended to shortly ? The present Government was made up of men who were thoroughly religious and who had at their head a man with a conscience which he dare not soil. (Cheers.) It was the best Government, in the sense that it was the most righteous. It was the most Liberal Govern- ment we ever had. He believed that the most famous Go- vernment which ruled for a few years after the passing of the first Reform Bill, and which succeeded in passing some very great and liberal measures, were not so liberal at heart as the present Government. Of course there had been difficulties in the way of legislation' and as much had not been done as ought to have been done, or as might have been done' and which the Government would have been willing to have done if the obstructionists had been out of the way. Some of the measures which had been passed, however, were of a Liberal and satisfactory character. One measure of religious liberty was the Burials Bill. • Of course that Act was not quite perfect. Acts generally required amendment. That Act, he considered, had been required to cure the obstinacy of some members of the Church of Eng- land. There always would be some persons who required such an Act before they did right, and he thought they ought to be grateful to the Government for the Burials Act. Then there was the Employers and Workmen's Act—a Bill for the benefit of working men and he would appeal to them whether that Act had not been of advantage to them. The first result of that Bill was 'to make the masters more careful. The Hares and Rabbits Bill wanted supplementing by giving the tenant full secu- rity for unexhausted improvements. Many farmers were deterred from killing ground game because if they did so they would be removed from their farms. He hoped the Government would pass the County Government Bill, be- cause it was hopeless to expect any relief of taxation so long as matters connected with county government were in such a muddle as they were now. Rates were levied half in one place and half in another, and nobody knew what he paid to. He only knew that he paid a great deal too much. (Laughter and hear, hear.) He claimed the farmers' sup- port. because for the last 10 or 12 years he had been con- sistent in advocating relief for them, and was not a tardy convert to compensation for unexhausted improvement such as his hon. opponent. He judged his opponent, of course, by his brother, the late member, who persistently opposed I him at the Cheshire Chamber of Agriculture on this question. He believed the farmers of Cheshire had been educated in recent years, and he confidently appealed to them for their support._ _

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT SANDBACH.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT SANDBACH.

The first meeting in furtherance of the candidature of the Hon. Alan de Egerton was held on Thursday night at San- bach. The Rev. J. R. Armistead, vicar of the parish, pre- sided ; and there was a large attendance.—The Hon. Alan Egerton, who was recsived with applause, said he hoped with Mr. Latham the contest would be fought on strictly political and not personal grounds. After condemning the foreign policy of the Government, he alluded to Irish affairs, and charged the Cabinet with the responsibility of .murders and of informers in Ireland. The time had now arrived when a stop must be put to the vacillating policy of the Government both at home and abroad.—Captain Ken- nedy, in a vigorous speech, proposed a resolution pledging the meeting to use its influence to secure the return of the Hon. Alan Egerton.—Mr. John Hague seconded, and the motion was carried with enthusiasm.

ANN-STREET LEVEL CROSSING, WIDNES, SPECIAL MEETING OF THE LOCAL A special meeting of Widnes Local Board was held on Monday evenieg, to receive a deputation with reference to the schemes propounded by the London and North-Western Railway Company arkil the.l3oard,kankalso to consider a re- port submitted by Mr: Johia Plerpoint regard to the sewerage scheme. Mr. F. 11. Gossage, the chairman, pre-. sided. There were also present Maus. F. H. Panknuret, D. Wright, Midwond. T. Handley, Forster, Dr. Booth, E. Carey, S. Sadler, Dr. O'Keeffe, Webster, Kershaw, Allen (clerk), and Higginson (surveyor). Mr. T. Cook and Mr. Robinson were present on behalf of the Widnes Foundry Company, and the ratepayers and property owners interested were represented by Messrs. Routledge, Carlisle. B. Dutton, T. G. Peters, S. Owens, W. Shaw, R. Hirst, W: Sadler, and others. In respouse to an intimation from the Chairman, Mr. THOMAS Coos remarked that he should like to ex- plain how the new road in place of Ann-street level crossing presented itself to the proprietors of Widnes Foundry Co. Though there was always a certain amourilEof inconvenience attending a level creasing, they were satisfied with the pre- sent road across the level crossing, but they understood the London and North-Western Railway Company wished to stop up -that level crossing, and substitute for it a uew road. It was proposed to carry the new road into Lugsdale- road, and after looking into the matter they thought the new road equal to the present road, and had no objection to it. Certainly there was the inconvenience of the gradients; but against this there was-the-inconvenience of the level crossing to which he had alluded, but they were of opinion that whoever took away the road from them must provide them with One ecival to that they already had. Now they understood the Local Board had signified their willingneee that the new road -should, under certain -conditions, stop at Victoria-street. Such a road would not be equal to their present road as far as Foundry Company's purpose was con- cernel They could not getttreir heavy traffic by the route proposed in the plan of the Board. They wished it to be understood, however, that they were not there for the pur- pose of interfering with the interests of the oroperty-owners in Ann-street. They had aepaelect right to defend their in- terests if they were imperilled, of course ; and they, on be e. half of the Foundry Company, had an equal right in rem, Act of the traffic in those !streets. . fie should like it • distinctly understood that they were not there for t' e AL pur- pose of objecting to the new street or the high lr down into Ann-street, and if the property owners in ,'.nat h,cality thought that their business was likely to be 'P lied, they were quite right to defend it. No doubt-in che case of Ann- street some portion of the traffic was diver'.ced, but ho thought the vehicular traffic .was not very great " and he thought that perhaps some arrangement could be . made with the railwaer company by which the foot passe- agers could get into Ann- street without very much troll, Jle. Their object in coming bet are the Board was to ask t nem to give their interests their serious consideration. P .e might remind them that the Foundry Company W` ere not inconsiderable ratepayers. They held that, thel-e road being taken away, they must have another sube.cituted, and they appeared before the Board to defend their interest in ti-is respect in the hope that the matter would receive consideration at the hands of the Board. vetOutessoN remarked that the Foundry Company u" 'Jot wish for a new road, but for a way into Lugsdale- ro:ad. --The •tieletitkeete : We shalt be glad to hear any represen- Ptations on the subject from any owners or occupiers in the - Alen-street district. _ ,- • Mr..RouTLEDGE, on behalf of the trustees Of. the late Mr. Atkins, objected to the scheme ,of the railway corn- parry ; .bnt if the branch to Ann-street was made they would not °Ned. • 'Mr.-OurEss 'appeared on behalf of Mrs. Singleton, who hadtteirishops in Ann-street, and said he considered that the interests of- -the Ann-street property .ovenere and the trustees to whom Mr. Rutledge had alluded were identical. He should be sorry to place himself in antagonism to the '''Ponsidry*CdmPatty ; but, Of course. they 'must maintain as 'fir as possible their Interests in Ann-street. The Foundry -Company•had told. them that they were considerable rate- payers, but their interests, he .considered, were very small indeed compared with those of Ann-street and the off streets. This was seen by comparing the assessment of the '• latter- *hick-was, hb foimd, £4,072,: with that of the Form- --eleyeaornpany, which was £6l. . , a Mr. T. J. Perna.s said lee had been instructed to ,appear een behalf of his client, Mr. John .Noon, who had a draper's .shop opposite to Victoria-street, and of Mrs. Price; who kept :the 'Market 'Gate' Hotel. The company's 'proposal; as he understbod it, was to put a stop to a road by -Act of Puha- - enent-,•and divert it into an altogether different direction, in enchs -way as he • thought there could no doubt whatever .e'eve-uld threaten the businesses in the locality with injury and ruin.. In fact, to carry out such a proposal would be to ..ruin_basiness, an 4 injuriously affect the interests of the property by an arrangement which was really intended for .the convenience of the railway' company; and such a pro- : .-po''Sal hemust stigmatise in the interests of his clients as a neOnstrthis one—(bear, hear)—since it was in effect to take aWrir the value from businesses and property without the least compensation. • His client -would pot object to the amended-plan of the Board. . . • Mr. WM. SADLER said he should prefer the level crossing to remain, but should object strongly to any scheme which *mita-rears Ann-sereet acus etc sac, • - - - • = Mr.Pillovravna, on behalf of her husband, who has pro- perty in Charlotte-stre,e4 objected to the railway company's • scheme. Mrs. JAMIESON, pawnbroker, Ann-street, also objected on the same grounds ; but, in reply to Mr. Carey, thought that the difficulty might be met by placing steps into the steed'. • • 'Mr. J. MATrusers said beeas a property owner in the dis- trict affeeted, must enter his protest against-, any schema that would tend to shut up Ann-street. He thought it was not for them to cry Ann-street is down; down with it.' (Laughter.) On the contrary, Ann-street was a business street, and was-inhabited by business people, and their in- terestnought riOt to be neglected—(hear, hear)—hut should be fairly dealt with by, the Board. He repudiated the idea Of steps,. to which there was a general objection. Even at , Runcorn Bridge they were doing away With them. , . Mr. CARLILE Said he thought the Board'sproposal a very good'one, and 'one that would commend itself to the great mijority of the ratepayers. Ile.did net think the,difficulties of the Widnes Foundry Company would be so great in re- gard to getting their boilers away by the route proposed in the plan of the. Board as they imagined. Mr. LEECH said he ' wai there" to' represent Dr: Gaskell, who Owned nine shops-id Ann-street, and who was of opinion that the railway company's scheme_ would prove very in- • jurioneindeed to his property. In fact, he felt sure it would •• • quite destroy. the streets as business streets, and so deteriorate I the value of the properly. • • - IldreWeLmaet &teat (Market Hotel) said he should prefer the road to remain as it was. ' • Mr. BetatErr Durrwr, who appeared on behalf of the executors of William Cooper, who owned shop, cottages, and ground rents of premisee. at the corner. of ,Victoria- - street, objected to -the proposal of the railway company on thelronnd of the injury that would result to property in the locality. They preferred the Local Board's' plan to the London and North-Western scheme, but would rather keep , the road as it was. He asked whether the new road pro- • posed wotild knock down the Catholic Chapel. Mr. KERSHAW : No. The Cumneeme : It simply knocks down some cottage property, and does not interfere with the Catholic Chapel. The_Board would give their consideration to the representa- tions Made td them, and were glad to have had the oppor- tunity of hearing both sides of the question—if there were two sides, though it was always their wish when possible as a-Board to reconoil conflicting interests and accommodate both. (Hear, hear.) • • • Mr. ,Coox thanked the Board for giving them an inter- ' 'teir;'ilid'observed:that-he hoped they would• take both sides- ' ' 'firtei'dellsideration. . • • • t 'The-various- representatives, of ,the owners aneratepayers -". " - interested then withdrew, ' Mr. Seanseitoobserved it wa,s, ,'stated that the Widnes Foundry Company paid as ranch in rates is all the-property owners put together. The Cs nutail remarked that even if that were so, it did hot follow that equal weight was to be attached to. them as a single body and the large number of other ratepayers affected, but that the interest of the larger flutaber had necessarily a claim upon them which could not be over- looked. - Mr. HANDLEY pointed out that it already had been shown that the property owners in question were assessed at £4,072, while the Foundry Company were assessed at

£761. Mr. KERSHAW said that as Chairman of the Highway Com- mittee he would 'move that, plan No. 1 (the scheme of the Board) be adhered to. • Dr.BOorn pointed ont.that there seemed to be unanimity on one point, both on the part of the Widnes Foundry Comvany and the other property. owners, viz., a preference for the existing, crossing, and asked why this should not be retained. - Mr. KERSHAW thought under existing circumstances it would net lot them to .prejudice themselves by ad- mitting the railway company's right to retaid the level crossing. Mr. WRIGHT thoUght the Board could not do better than press forward No. 1 plan and seconded Mr. Kershaw's motion to that effect: • • The motion was carried. THE SEWERAGE SCHEME.—MR. COPELAND'S SALARY. Mr. PIERPOINT, of 'Warrington, who has been appointed resident engineer pro tem. in connection with the sewerage scheme, presented a report as to the present condition of the sewer, and the difficulties which have arisen with the con- tractor: Mr. himwoon asked whether, supposing that Mr. Cope- land would be likely te remain ill for a lengthy period, sly six months, it was the intention of the Board to pay him his present salary, which, as it was, amounted to something like £2OO a__year. Mr. HANDLEY pointed out that the illness from which Mr. Copeland was suffering had taken place during his service to the Board. The CHAIRMAN said that no doubt the matter would have to be considered, but at present they had no means of judg- ing how long Mr. Copeland would be absent from his duties, and that being so, they could not, under present circum- stances, take any action in the matter. Mr. Pizik,POINT then explained his report in detail to the Board, and remarked that he had had an interview with Mr. Jeffries, who seemed desirous of settling the matter. After some discussion it was decided that Mr, Pierpoint

THE REV, PETER 3IACKENZIE AT WIDNES. LECTURE ON THE TONGUE. With the object of increasing the circuit funds of tii6• Widnes Wesleyan Circuit the Rev. Peter MacKenzie p:eached in Victoria-road Wesleyan chapel on Thursday to a good congregation. In the evening a large audience as- sembled to hear Mr. MacKenzie lecture on "The tongue : its use and abuse." Mr. Thomas occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Revs. R. Harper and J. Tesseyman, Messrs. B. Brown, R. Fogg, T. Sadler, and Mr. Clark. .The Chairman briefly introduced The LECTURER, who, after remarking that the chairman looked sunny, spoke honey, and was always good at giving money (laughter and applause) said they had without doubt chosen a very popular subject—it was in every body's mouth. (Laughter.) They knew that in the first five days of the Creation, when the Lord was clothing the earth with light and beauty—covering it with myriads of vegetable and and animal life, the world was still and voiceless. But by, and bye man was made—the masterpiece of creation—the the wondrous connecting link between nothing and the Deity. Man was made a power, a thing of life a wise and glorious creature, with every gift that Ge-',„ could endow him. He endowed him with the "'itt of speech, and the internal fires of the new-form -.ed. cleatare beginning to burn, the silence was brol-en, an rea ii:T . d c t thrilled with the eloquence of sr -- cally defenceless compared - • ,eech. Men were physt- but they bad that now . eat& some of the brute creation, • --J - - - ,ek which proved their supetiority to any of the brute creation, for life and death ,were in the power ot the tongue. With an edge as keen aft rt razor, with a point as sharp as a spear, Iwith a. sarcasm as scathing as the lightning's flash, and with .e'ccnenee as sympathetic as a river of oil and as Pleasing as the notes of the nightingale, what a wonderful power bad '.we tongue'. Everybody, from the prince to the beggar, stood in need of that little instrument the tongue. As the , eye revealed the glorious beauties of the natural world, so I 13 pe ecla revealed the hidden man, drew the soul out of its dark recesses, made thoughts visible, and ideas palpable; for speech was the voice of the human soul, it was the pump which brought up the water out of the great lake of thought. What a wonderful thing was speech. and what results it had pro- duced. He described the tongue as a little instru- ment, six inches by two, and said a woman was given the name of "Mum' on account of her well-known love of silence. (Loud laughter.) ;There being such power in the [ tongue it was important that we should regulate it properly. ' In the Proverbs, in Solomon, in the discourses of our Lord, and in the epistles of James, the government of the tongue was made a matter of supreme importance in personal religion. Foreigners said that Englishmen were taciturn, but although that might bathe rule, there were a tremendous lot of exceptions to it. (Loud laughter.) There were people, who like a river, were always emptying themselves by the mouth. (Laughter.) They gave an ocean of talk without a drop of sense in it. Old men were talkative for want of memory, and young men for want of wit. (Laughter.) They must he careful with the unruly member. Five words cost Zacharias forty weeks' silence. It was a terrible lesson to him not to cross-question the preacher next time he had the chance. (Laughter and applause.) Just as heat ex- pands and coal contracts iron bodies, so was it natural for man to speak the things which he had seen and heard. God liked a man to keep giving what he had learned and studied himself. He had still as much left for himself. The bene- fits of rational conversation were incalculable for himself. Passing on to some of the abuses, the rev, gentleman said lying was a great abuse of the tongue. "A liar we can never trust, though he should tell the thing that's true, and he that tells a lie at first, then tries to hide it, makes it two." It was the best thing in the world to tell the truth; it was a poor thing to lie. Mr. MacKenzie spoke of the importance of parents speaking the truth to their children, and keeping all promises faithfully with them. Never give out for a fact what they had only from hearsay, or conjecture, or opinion—" Lest men suspect your tale -untrue, keep probability in view." What an awkward thing it would be if the telegraph was to take to fibbing through some inherent depravity in the electric fluid. (Laughter.) Suppose Mr. Harper telegraphed to New- castle-on Tyne for six barrels of oysters for the delectation of the circuit stewards' the local preachers and the rest of the officials of the Widnes circuit, and through that fibbirig wire there were actually sent six hogsheads of treacle! (Loud laughter.) He would never outlay another shilling on that fibbing wire as long as it stood on wooden legs. (Renewed laughter.) The evils of swearing were touched upon, and, referring to evil speaking, Mr. MacKenzie said it was not evil speaking to reprove a person for a fault at the right time and in a right temper ; but to reprove a small fault with undue severity, was as much out of place as taking a hammer to knock a fly off a . friend's forehead. The cure was considerably worse than the oirginal disease. Another abuse of the little member was that of detraction, by which he meaut—lowering a little bit, taking down a peg, &c. Let them look to the best side of a man's character and not to the worst. If they could not get the , wheat without the chaff let them be thankful there was no I more chaff. Tale-beariog was a business engaged in for the last 6,000 years, and there had never been a fresh license taken out. (Laughter.) Tale-bearers were the devil's post- men—(laughter)—and the biggest sycophants; and slander was hell's foulest fiend, and murder its employer. If a man slandered them, he was either a friend, an enemy, or a disinterested person. Speaking of flattery, the lecturer said it was an old maxim at.the schools, that "flattery is the food of fools," but now and then their men of wit would condescend to take a bit. Flattery was deceptive, damaging, dangerous. If a man that flattered them had not deceived them, he was going to do. (Laughter.) His advice was, don't flatter anyone, but give honour to whom honour was due. After a humorous reference to the grumblers, Mr. MacKenzie concluded by saying that if they were good and true and pure, the Master's smile would rest upon them, and when the tongue was silent in this life, they would join together in the song of Moses and of the Lamb for ever and ever, in a brighter and fairer region. (Loud applause.) -A vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. MacKenzie for his lecture, and a similar compliment having been paid to the chairman, the meeting concluded.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES DRAPER.
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES DRAPER.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. Hol- brook Gaskell, senr., and Mr. George Pilkington' Patrick O'Connor, tailor and woollen draper, formerly of Church- street, was brought up under a warrant, charged with attempting to defraud his creditors by removing a certain part of his property after, or four months previous to, filing his petition in liquidation. Mr. Stananonght (Messrs. Yate- i son and Stananought) appeared to prosecute. He said the prisoner had for some years carried on in Widnes the busi- ness.of a tailor and draper. In December last he filed his petition in liquidation in Liverpo 1 Bankruptcy Court,.and he offered to arrange for a composition with his creditors. On the 16th January the first meeting of creditcrs was held, and it was decided that liquidation by arrangement should take place. Mr. S. Tilsey, of Manchester, was appointed trustee of the estate. It was now alleged that previous to Ri- sing his petition the prisoner clandestinely removed a quantity of his good from his shop, and forwarded them to the ' residence of his brother, Martin O'Connor, at Car- , raduff, County Roscommon, Ireland. The prisoner would also be charged under sub-section one of the 11th section of the Debtor's Act with not having discovered all his goods to the.trustee appointed under the liquidation; also under sub-section two of the same section, with not delivering the property in his custody to. his creditors; and further, under sub-section four; with concealing his goods.—Mr. Graskell asked the prisoner if he was legally represented.—The pri- soner replied that he instructed Mr. Stananought on behalf, but he ,now found that oentleman was solicitor to the trustee as well as executor to- the man from whom he bought his goods.—Mr. Stananought remarked that the pri- soner instructed him to flle his petition. of liquidation, but 'at the first meeting of , creditors he was appointed solicitor to the trustees, and fioding that the prisoner had clandestinely removedhis goods he declined to have any- thing further•to do with him,—Mr. VYaltealliso Messenger of Liverpool County Court, having produced the file of Liquidation proceedings, Martin Connor was called. He said he lived at 9arraduff, County Roscommon, Ireland. At • the request of the prisoner he camito'Widnes on the 23rd December. The., prisoner told him that he had sent some goods to TreTand, and they arrived at Roscommon on the day he (witness),left that place. By the directions of his brother (the prisoner), he packed up a number of bales of gords, and removed part of them to the beerheuse in Wel- lington-street, kept by a man named Tansley, and part to the house of a man named Stafford, One right (he didn't know the date) he went to Liverpool, intending to go to Ireland, with seven bales of cloth, several cases containing two clocks, a pier glass, pictures, &c. The prisoner helped to pack the goods 'up, and it was dark when they removed them. He intended to ship, them at Liverpool for Ros- common. The goods were seized by the Liverpool police. —The prisoner said his brother's statement was true; and be was than remanded until Thursday nest.

, TEMPERANCE MEETING AT WESTON. -In connection with the Runcorn Circuit Wesleyan Methodist Temperance Sockty, a meeting was held on Monday, at the Wesleyan schools, Weston Point, under the presidency of Mr. Riad. Clarke. Appropriate addresses on temperance topics were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. S. C. Beckett, the Rev. Geo. Hack, and Mr. J. R. Frith. At the close of the meeting, which had been very enthusiastic, 61 new pledges were taken, and it was decided to at once establish a Band of Hope.

UNITED FREE CIIIIRCH, OMELAND•STREET, WIDNES.— The annual sermons in aid of the United Free Church Home and Foreign Missions were preached in the above place of worship .n Sunday last, by the Rev. J. Billington. There were good congregations, at each service, and collec- tions were taken. On Tuesday evening the annual mis- sionary meeting was held, and there was a large audience. Mdressee were delivered by the Revs. J. Sarvent, of St. Helens, J. Peters, Congregational, Widnes, and J. Billing- ton, the pastor.

RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.

The half-yearly meeting of Ike shareholders of the Runcorn' Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company was held in the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday afternoon. In the absence of Mr. John Brundrit, the Chair. man of directors, who it was stated .was ill, Mr. William Hayes, of Ashton Hayes, presided. There were also present :—Messrs. J. Simpson, W. Whitaker, T. Banks, E. Timmins, T. Norman, James Collier, -James Shaw, and • /Q. W. T. ‘retary). the report was presented as follows:—" The directors have convened the half-yearly meeting of shareholders, to be held in their offices' the Public Hall, Runcorn, on Monday, the 26th day of Feb- ruary, at half-past three o'clock precisely. The revenne account shows a balance of £467 us. 3d., including 07 17s. 84., brought forward from the previous half -yell', but of which the :directors recommend :a dividend.to be paid of three pounds ten shillings per centum per annum, free of income tax, payable on and after the let day of March' • this will absorb £437 14s , leaving a balance of £29 17s. 3d. to be carried forward. The heavy rainfall during the past three months of the year 1882 has enabled parties to sup- ply themselves with water to some extent without purchas- ing it from the Company, consequently the last quarter's receiptsior water eupplied by ineter Was the least of any in the year; but the Supply to Muse property continues to in- crease, and mninl arc extended to newly—erected houses as Pie!' are required. The gales in January last did a little ..njury to the engine house roof, on the Heath, which will be covered by ten pounds, but with that exception all the buildings, machinery, and plant, are in good order." The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report and the payment of the dividend, as recommended, referred to the heavy rainfall, remarking that the London and North- Western -Railway Co. had. taken an unusual small quantity of water, because with a good rainfall they could store suffi- cient for their purpose. There had been a continuous increase in the demand for water for house property. The small householders were the best customers of the oornly.ny, and while benefiting themselves benefited the comp'any.— Mr. T. &oars seconded the motion, which was unanimously carried.—Mr. T. NORMAN moved that the bee, thanks of the shareholders be given to the directors for their services during the last half-year, and also to the secretary.—Mr. Commix seconded the niotion.—lt was carried unani- tnoosly.—The CHAIRMAN replied.—On the motion of Mr. SHAW, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and the meeting terminated.

Mr. B IiNiVETON was called upon to move the first re- solution, as follows :—" That this meeting, in view of the present critical condition of the agricultural interest through- out the country, hails with pleasure the liberal and en- lightened views of Mr. G. W. Latham, on the Land Ques- tion, and on the subject of social and political reform, as expressed in his electoral address and speeches; and is of opinion that he is a fit and proper person to represent Mid- Cheshire in Parliament, and pledges itself to use its best efforts to secure his triumphant return at the ensuing elec- tion."—Mr. Kniveton, in moving the resolution, delivered a spirited and telling speech upon the land question, ad- vocating an improved system of land tenure, so that the land, should be capable of producing half as much again as it was doing at the the present time. If the restrictions which now weighed down the agricultural interest were removed, capital and labour would be used to a greater extent than they now were. Increased produce would mean diminished prices, and therefore the working classes would be put in a position to live with more comfort, and partake of a few of the luxuries of life. The farmers too would be greatly bene- fitted. But there would never be a reform in the Land Laws until it was forced from the Legislature by public opinion, and if there was an improvement to take place in the Land Laws it would have to begin with the Liberal party in the House of Commons. (Cheers.) They mast ha i e persons sent to Parliament who were prepared to legislate for the benefit of the people, and not for a class, and in Mr. Latham they had a man who was prepared to do so. (Cheers.) Mr. J. R. FRITH seconded the motion, dealing with the franchise question in a way which freqnently elicited cheers. Mr. W. HANDLEY supported the motion, and referring to the passage in Mr. Alan Egerton's address, which stated that he was in favour of relieving the agricultural interest by obtaining some contribution towards the local rates from that claas of property so unfairly exempt, said it was an attempt by its vagueness to create a false impression. Mr. Handley pointed out that in towns owners had to do repairs to their property and to form efficient works of sewerage, but in the country the farmer had to do all this, and was thus heavily handicapped. Mr. Egerton also Said he should be prepared when the proper time came to form an opinion. (Laughter.) They wanted men whose opinions were already formed, and who could tell what he thought on certain great questions that must come; and what he would do in regard to them. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Latham declared, on the other hand, what he was prepared to do, and they believed he had the energy and the power to do it. (Cheers.) He (Mr. Handley) believed that Mr. Latham initiated the reforma- tory system into Cheshire, and for many years he kept Bradwell Reformatory open at his own expense—(cheers)— in order to do away with juvenile crime by reform instead of by punishment. (Cheers.) In a few years it was seen that that was the principle that juvenile crime ought to be dealt with, and the county took over Bradwell Reformatory as a public institution. (Cheers.) The Liberals meant to be victorious in this contest; but if they did not win, they should not lose heart and spirit. They would try, try again, for they knew that they would win if time was given them; but he thought victory would come within the next fortnight. (Cheers.) He would conclude by quoting a verse which he thought would inspirit them : Shout! shout! and work for victory, Each voter on the roll; Both youth and age so hoary Go boldly to the poll; Then in this Ird-division We'll show we're marching on, And our Cheshire's exclamation Will be "Bravo, lads ! well done."
'Cheers.)

The resolution was passed with one or two dissentients. On the motion of Mr. T. HANDLEY, seconded by Mr. R. SHAW, a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, and the meeting concluded. It was announced that Mr. Latham would address the electors in the same room, on Tuesday afternoon, at two o'clock.

the past year, stated that during the year 1882 therd were I registered 159 births, of which 88 were males and 71 females. In the same period 118 deaths were registered. The excess of births over deaths was 41, or at the rate of 8 8 per 1,000 of the resident population. The annual birth rate was 34.0 compared with an average of 31-3, and the death-rate was 25-2 com- pared with a former average of 105. The high death-rate had teen occasioned by two complaints—measles and whoop- ing cough, both largely fatal when epidemic amongst young children, having been present during the second and third quarters of the year. It was only usual that where coin- plaint 9 of the zymotic class had been widespread that there should be a correspondingly high infantile death-rate from general causes, and it should be the effort of a community to minimise as much as possible the conditions inimical to life and health to which he alluded. In no year after the completion of the. waterworks had more important sanitary work been done by the local anthority of Lymm than in that just passed. In addition to improvements in the sani- tary arrangements of many private dwellings, a large portion of the district had been laid out for a modern and efficient system of sewerage, with a new and well-appointed outfall. A complete sanitary survey of the town had been made, and the thanks of the department were rendered to the medical men in the district who gave information, and generally ended with much cordiality and efficiency in re- pressing such centres of infection as frem time to time were discovered. The fact that only three out of 118 deaths were from diarrhea was a sufficient testimony to the con- tinued purity of the water, a sanitary anal ysis of which ac- compained the report.

div.head: FRODSFIAM MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: FRODSFIAM MUSICAL SOCIETY.

JUDAS MACCAREUS. The Frodsham Musical Society gave their last concert of this tte-ason in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Wednesday evening, when Handel's oratoria entitled Judas Maccabstus, was listened to by a crowded audience. The principals were Miss Emily Stewart, Miss Lizzie Lambert, Mr. Arthur Tuer, and Mr. Henry Cuzner. Mr. Powell was the leader of the band, and the chorus consisted 6! about 60 Yoices, under the conductorship of Mr. Argent. The argument of the oratorio is as follows : Mattathias, the leader of the Jews, is dead. and the people mourn for his loss. The Divine guidance is invoked, and Judas, the son of Hattathlas. Is elected as chief of the people. who, trusting in God. prepare themselves for battle. War Is made against Appollonius, Governor of Samaria, and Berm. Governor of •Ccelesyria ; and victory is the result. While4the people are yet celebrating the. triumphs of Judas, news is brought that Georgias, commander of part of the Syrians, is again in arms, and the Israelites are dismayed. Judas calls once more upon his followers, and hastens to the battle-field. laaving behind him others to worship and pray in the TemPle: Finally, Judas returns again victorioui, and the people cele- brate his prowess, and praise God who has given them ;the victory. Miss Emily Stewart as soprano, gave the recitatives and airs in a manner which showed that she had f all confidence in the rote she had undertaken, and the difficult passages were rendered with correctness of expression, and distinct vocalization, particularly in the air containing some diffi- cult variations, and commencing with the words "So shall the lute and harp awake." Miss Lizzie Lambert, contralto, has appeared in Frodabam on many occasions, but has never been heard to better advantage than ' on Wednesday evening, her best effort being In part 3, commencing with "Father of Heaven, from Thy eternal thrOne," it being a prayer fora blessing upon the preparation to solemniz the feast of lights. The devotional and pleading character im - parted to the piece merited the highest praise, and was duly appreciated by the audience. Mr Henry Cuzner has a plea- sant voice; and sang with artistic taste, his rendition of the air " Arm, armi ye brave," directing the people to prepare for battle, being his most successful effort. Mr. Trier, the 1 tenor, did fairly well, and sang correctly. We think, how- ever, he must have been suffering from a cold as his un- certain style of giving " Sound an alarm" detracted some- what from the excellent chorus which followed, his voice being wanting in the fire and force which should character- ize the leader of a fighting host. The choruses were given in a praiseworthy manner, but the trebles were rather severely handicapped by the weight of the other parts; this was not a very serious defect considering that it was due to the excellence of the other parts of the chorus; taken as a whole the choruses went well. "See the conquering hero comes," with the orchestral accompaniment, being loudly ap- pliuded, and secured an encore. The band performed their part judiciously, and were quite up to the mark. Mr. Argent wielded the baton with his usual ability, and added to the musical effect by his accompaniment on the harmonious.

div.head: SWINE FEVER IN WIDNES.
div.p: SWINE FEVER IN WIDNES.

A BUTCHER HEAVILY FINED. At Widnes Petty Eessions, on Wednesday, John Miller, butcher, Ann-street West, was summoned that having in his possession ou Thursday, The 22nd February, a pig affected with swine fever, he did neglect to give notice of the same to the police. He was further charged with unlawfully removing, or causing to be removed, to Tarbock a pig which had died of swine fever. Patrick Carrot was charged with having, on the 22nd February, committed an offence under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by throwing a pig which had died from swine fever into a pool at Tarbock.— Mr. J. 0. Swift defended Miller.—Carrol pleaded guilty, but Superintendent Barker said he would withdraw the informa- tion against him, because he thought he had simply been a was at first inter_ded to take the cases separately, but after the first one had been partially inquired into, it was decided to take the summonses together. Carrol was called as a witness, and said he had, been in the employ of the defendant for twelve months. His duty was to feed the pigs and attend to the horse of the defendant. On Wednesday, the 21st February, the defendant had 17 pigs on the premises, and on the evening of that day they were all well; but on Thursday morning, when he went to feed the pigs, he found that one was dead. He in- formed the defendant, who afterwards saw the dead pig, and directed the witness to put it into a bag, the horse in the trap, and convey away the dead pig, and to throw it into some old ditch or pit He drove by Stockswell to Tarbock, where he threw the pig into a pit of water situated in a field off the lane. When he returned he told the defendant what he had done, and he said it was all right if the pig was in a Pit or ditch. On Sunday morning, the 25th ult., witness pointed out the pit to P.C. Rutherford, who pulled out the pig, which witness identified He should not have taken the pig from the premises had not the defendant ordered him to do so.—By Mr. Swift: Defen- dant did not see the pigs on the Wednesday.—Mr. Welsby, jun., veterinary surgeon, said he accompanied Superinten- dent Barker to a field at Tarbock on Saturday, and saw there a pie, of which he made a post-mortem examination. It had died of swine fever. There were external marks on the pig, which perfectly satisfied him before he opened the animal, that the pig had died of swine fever.—By Mr. Swift : A pig might die from fever in twelve hours.— Thomas Berry, farmer, larbock,,said the pool into which the pig was thrown was much used. His cattle drank from the water, which flowed all through the township, and near all the farms in the district. The farmers used it for their cattle because it was such fresh water. In some places the -water was, used for domestic purposes. He kept a number of pigs, and when he saw the dead pig in ,the pool he was'' much `afraid.— Inspector Barnett deposed that about 8-30, on Saturday night last, he went to the defendant's shop. , He told the: defendant about the pig, and asked what he was going to do. He replied that he did not know, and after consider- able hesitation he added "I did it for the best; but it seems for the-worst." In answer to the inspector he said be had. 16 pigs all in goed health except one which Pad been "taking fits " that day. -The inspector then took Carrel into custody, and returning to the defendant's premises, half an hour after midnight, he found a dead pig there. On Monday morning he again 'went to the premises, and tound. another pig dead. The defendant had never given any information of the swine fever.—Mr. Welaby, senior, ve,erinary inspector for Widnes division, said he had made a post-mortem examination of the two pigs referred to by the inspeztor. They had died of swine fever.—Mr. Swift, in defence, contended that there had been no legal proof of the issuing of the order of the Privy Council declaring swine fever a disease -ender the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act; and, therefore, the defendant could not be said to have been guilty of ony offence. The instructions given to Carrel . by the defendant were to bury the pig where there were no cattle. The defendant had no reason for burying the pig in, the pit; he had every reason for adopting some other place of burial. He was not aware that the pig had suffered from fever, and he disposed of the carcase, as he thought, in the safest possible manner. It would be a hardship if he were made to suffer for his man's carelessness. If the defendant had wished to do anything improper he could have got rid of the pig in his own shop, but he had no desire to do any- thing wrong. That was a point in his favour. By the Act of Parliament the defendant could claim one half of the value of the pigs up to 40s if pigs that had died through disease were buried by order of the court, and if the defendant had had any idea that these pigs were suffering from fever, and had known that it was necessary to give information to the police, would not he have done so and claimed his com- pensation? Did not these facts speak strongly in favour of the innocence of the defendant, and satisfy their worships that he did not mean to do anything wrong.—Mr. Gaskell said the Bench had decided to convict in both cases. The magistrates thought the defendant very much to blame for not giving notice to the police when he had on his premises three pies which were ill, and which eventually died. His offence was much aggravated by the course he pursued with regard to the first pig which died. He (Mr, (+askell) could not conceive of a worse case. It was highly improper to Wage a diseased pig in a pond where cattle were drinking regularly, and which was connected with a brook which ran through the township, and was used by many farmers. The

div.head: CONSERVATISM AT LYMA.
div.p: CONSERVATISM AT LYMA.

On Mondry, the adjourned annual meeting of Lymm Constitutional and Conservative Association was held in the Clubroom, under the presidency of Dr. Brabazon. There was a very good attendance. • Mr. RICHARD S3IITH (hon. secretary) read the report for the year 1882, as follows :—" The pest year has been a year of progress for the Lymm Constitutional and Conservative Association, which is now well equipped for the purpose of a central organization for the supporters of constitutional principles in the polling district. The news-room and library continue to be largely used, but the committee again ' feel compelled to draw the more general attention of the members to these advantages. The billiard table has proved pvular, and the returns from it are in excess of the expenditure. The annual tea party and entertainment, held at the Plough Assembly Room, was very successful, being attended by more than 300 members and friends. The committee tender their i thanks to the ladies who contributed trays, and those who assisted at the eritertainment, as well as to Mr. Tone Nash 1 for his effective address on the political topics of the day.' The ball arranged under the auspices of the associa- tion was well attended and highly appreciated. The com- mittee are anxious still further to entend the usefulness of the association by enrolling on the list of members all in- habitants of the district who feel interested in the mainte- nance and diffusion of constitutional and Conservative prin- ciples. The news-room and library are open freely to all members, and the premises have been recently enlarged by the addition of a room suitable for social gatherings and lectures. Friends of the Conservative cause cannot do better service to the principles they advocate than by at once allying themselves with the reorganised organisation of the party in their district." Mr. ARDERN (the treasurer) read the statement of ac- counts, which showed a balance of £6 2s 41-d to the credit of the association. There were, however, some unpaid accounts which would leave them £l5 is old in debt; but against this there were a few arrears of subscriptions. Mr. CALLENDER moved the adoption of the report and the treasurer's statement of accounts.

Mr. G. HALL seconded, and speaking with regard to the progress of the club, said he was certain everyone in that room would agree with him that, taking into consideration the ostensible purposes for which that club was formed, the progress had not been so satisfactory as it ought to have been. They ought to have more assistance from lectures. During the last year they had had no more than one lecture. He believed it was the duty, and it was also the intention from the first, of that club to educate the public mind to similar views they themselves maintained. On that ground they had been very remiss, and he hoped sincerely that in future greater efforts would be made to promulgate those grand principles which belonged to their constitution. Mr. R. SMITH remarked that he did not _think really there was any difference of opinion on the matter. They all felt it was exceedingly desirable to have from time to time lectures and addresses on Conservative politics, but it must be remembered that up to the present time they had no room of their own adapted for the purposes of a lecture. Their funds also had not justified them in going outside to hire a room, and in placarding and advertising. It could not be done for less than £3, and they were not quite in the position of their Radical friends, who had subscriptions (which he thought were not legally subscribed)available at any time for lectures. The motion was carried. _ _

Colonel Legh was appointed president of the association; Mr. Peter Stubs, vice-president; Mr. Ardern, treasurer ; Messrs. Callender, Collin Mclver, J. P. Legh, John Marsh, Joseph Smith, Richard Smith, J. Read, Newton, Dayley, Sandie, T. P. Norris, Swallow, John Ardern,and J. Gregson, committee; and Messrs. P. Stubs and R. Smith were ap- pointed to represent the association on the Central Com- mittee.
A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the meeting to a close.
LYMM LOCAL BOARD.
The monthly meeting was held on Thursday. Present: Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Dewhurst, Rogers Cal- lender, Forster, Gibbon, Appleton, Taylor, and Ridgway (clerk).

div.head: SANITARY.
div.p: SANITARY.

A report prepared by Dr. Fox (medical officer), at the request of the Board, was read by the Cul.aume.N. It stated the number of houses was 1,017, privies 1,008, w.c.'s in houses 91, water closets in yards 23, pails 63, covered cess- pits 344, open cesspits 39, covered ashpits 121, open ash- pits 240. It had Oen computed that as many as 90 per cent of injurious nuisances were formed in connection with privies or privy arrangements, and it was a further fact be- yond doubt that of all nuisances of whatever kind, or from whatever source, those from festering excrement were the distinctly poisonous, and were known to convey directly the seeds of specific disease. Dr. Fox pointed out that the first and most effective step in the way of sanitary improvement was in the direction of privy accommodation. The pail system had certain advantages, but where the house was connected with the sewer Fowler's modified water closet pan offered the best and cheapest method of solving the difficulty. It was desirable that householders within the reach of the sewer should abolish their old-fashioned privies, and make the necessary alterations. It was decided that the report be printed and circulated among the ratepayers. SANITARY REPORT. This report stated that there were. a few cases of scarlet fever in the town. Papers had been served and precautionary measures taken against the spread of the disease. MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNEAL REPORT. Dr. J. M. Fox (medical officer), in big annual report for
