THE FEET 71; IN RUNCORN. • The decision 4 soj contest the division was receiVe with unbounded imtisfaction and enthusiasm by the vxtuncorn Libs on Wednesday morning. All the maohi"aery neces- sary for fighting a successful election camPair,n was in per- fect working order, and at the word of cot- nmand could at once be set in motion. Early on Wednesday morning the town was posted Mr. Latham's address, and with a placard Cuing a meeting of,i electors and non-electors the same was held, and speeches were de' evening. That meeting 4 de' by several leading te Liberals to a large and enth mously pledged themselves nastic audience, who unani- `.c. use every effort during the presentcelection to secure PA.. Latham's election to Parlia- ment. The accomplish rup at of that desired end is considered I assured by each indivio ,ual member of the party. With the increased popularity of Mr. Latham among the fanning classes, ' the tine .„allable most position of the Government, and a favourable register they confidently I declare that v sctory is nigh, and truly they are sparing nol pains to wave! t that prediction into a certainty. The corn-1 modlons premises of Mr. C. Houghton, in High-street, have been e`sigaged as the Liberal committee rooms, and they ars sotr.ounded by many signs of animation. Here the busines, o't the Runcorn Polling District, which includes Runcorn, Halton, Weston, Stockham, Sutton, Clifton, Moore, Norton, and Kekewick, will be transacted, and clerks and canvassers have been hard at work since Wednesday. Over £lOO has been subscribed by the leading Liberals to defray the local expenses ofethe contest. In direct contrast to this satisfactory state of things, is the dis- organised condition of the Tory party in the town. They were not prepared for a contest, when the news of the election broke in upon them, and it is ramouret that there is a split in the camp. In the Parish Church Schools, on Monday evening, they held what a contemporary terms a " crammed and enthusiastic" meeting of electors. The literal accuracy of one part of the phrase is amusing. Crowded the meeting was, for about thirty of the loyal upholders of Church and State were packed in a room about twelve feet square; but the proceedings, far from being "enthusiastic," were what ia usually described as "lively." The public are denied the enjoyment of perusing a full account of the pro- ceedings but it was palitely intimated to the memberof the press who pat in an appearance that the eloquence which was expected to flow was "not for publication." However, a gentleman whose public duties occasionally take him to the Burial Board, attacked his party right and left, and we be- lieve has declined to act with them during the contest. He rated them soundly on their want of organisation, and even went so far as to charge the Conservatives, in the Commis- sioners' Chamber, with neglecting the public benefit in watching the interests of a private firm. Eventually, this free lance of the party was ruled out out of order in his remarks, and canvassers were appointed , to districts, the meeting concluding with the passing of a resolution in sup- port of the candidaturs of the Hon. Alan Egerton: On Tuesday evening next the Liberal candidate, Mr. a. W. Latham, will address the electors in Runcorn Public Hall. The meeting will be presided over by Mn Robert Shaw, the president of the Liberal Association, and the Hon. Lyulph, Stanley, M.P., Mr. J. Howard, M.P., Mr. H. H. Fowler, M.P., Mr. W. S. Caine, •M.P., and others are ,ex- pected to deliver addresses. We , understand that. it IS in contemplation to hold meetings at Halton and Weston on the afternoon of 'the same day, in order to give Mr. Latham an opportunity of addressing the tenant farmers in those districts. . , •

div.head: LATHAM OR EGERTON ?
div.p: LATHAM OR EGERTON ?

A. WORD TO THE ELECTORS OF MID-CHESHIRE. Fellow Electors,—Perinit me to address a few ,words to you in regard to the contest in which we are now engaged. has come upon us suddenly and unexpectedly, but, I yen- , ture to think, it has not found us, like the foolish virgins, , with our lamps gone out. We have kept the lamp of , knowledge burning, and in its light we know our man, and , are prepared to give him our, hearty and united ,support. The Conservatives, at a very funereal gathering, held at Itnutsfordi decided upon the Hon. Alan Egerton as their , candidate. The Lib_rals, assembled at Altrincham from all parts of the division, resolved with the greatest unanimity and enthusiasm to adhere to their old and true friend Geo. William Latham. These two gentlemen are the candidates for the honour of being our representative in the British Parliament. Which shall we choose? Who shall be our M.P., Latham or L'gerton ? The addresses of both• candi- dates are now in our hands, and, I would hope, have been carefully perused by every, enfranchised man. It may be said that between the two addresses there is not a com- parison, only a contrast. The one in blue as manly,, out- spoken, and distinguished by a clear conception of tha kind of legislation w ~ich the exigencies of the times demand. That is worthy of Latnam ! But what shall I say of the address which is printed in glaring red ink ? It is puerile, , evasive, and affords not the slightest indication that its honourable author .underatandetho wanta of the lltitiab people. What else could be expected from an Egerton! But the candidates shall speak for themselves.. In the first paragraph of his address the Hon. Alan Egerton says, 'Though I have not been constantly resident among you, I am not unknown to many of the Electors."' What a contrast that presents to the following from the address of the Liberal candidate :—" My opinions are so well known to you that I need not trouble you by stating them at any length. I have lived among you now for over thirty years." Mr. Egerton is not unknown. But Mr. Latham is so well known. The former is a bird of paradise, clothed in the brilliant plumage of the Metropolitan Board of works, and, it is evident, he thinks his gay feathers will win him many votes. 'Tis true that he has favoured as with a song, but the tones are so very uncertain that we are compelled to regard it as an imitation, aud not as an original composition. Ti P latter is one of the genuine home-birds of Britain. His p,umage is not _at all gay, but his song is sweet, and his toue,s are clear and unflattering. We have long been Litni:i 1r with his voice, and have been charmed with the excellent quality of, his songs. A constituency is sometimes compelled by circumstances to choose a comparative stranger as its 'representative. But in our case no such circumstances exist. We have before US a genuine Cheshire yeoman, who, for thirty years has gone in and otit amongst us as a familiar friend. His light has not been hid in the fogs of the Metropolitan Board of Works, but at agricultural gatherings and Chambers of Commerce he .has expressed his views with lucidity and. force. Therefore, he is the man whom we should send to St. Stephen',s at the present juncture.

There is already in the . Honse Of Commons a sufficient number of dummies, iquirelings, and' honourables who seem incapable of anything but obstruction. For Britain's sake, then, let us not add another to that useless number. Will the tenant-farmers of Mid-Cheshire bear in mind that during the present session of Parliament their interests will occupy a foremost place in the deliberations of the House of Commons. Which of the two candidates is likely to afford the most le 1p ? It ought not to be difficult to decide' ttrat question now that their respective views are laid before us. What does the Hon. Alan Egerton say ? "I am in favour of immediate legislation which would secure to the tenant- farmer, where, he has not already obtained it by agreement with his landlord, such compensation for unexhausted improvements as would encourage the inves'ment of capital in the soil."• Now, of all points, this is the one in which he ought to have been most explicit. But his'paragraph on the matter is nothing more than a clever evasion. Ought he not to have told us what, in his ()Pinion, is' the sort of legislation which will secure to the tenant-farmer, compensation for unhauSted improve- ments? Compare this weak and inexplicit utterance with the straightfordward deliverance of Mr. Latham, who says, "I' am convinced-that no bill on this subject will be ad- equate that does not contain provision that no tenant should leave his farm without full payment for. what he has ex- pended in raising its letting Value, and which We has not got back; that no sitting tenant should.have hi & rent raised upon his own improvements; and that there shotild be full freedom of sale and culture. I would most earnestly sup- port a bill containing the..se provhsions, and feel sure that theTtnay be enrried out, without, infringing the rights of the owners of the soil." After reading that statement we cermet have anydonbt as to what,in Mr.Latham's opinion, will secure compensation to the tenant farmers.-- And is it not tolerably certain from his political confession and family connection thatiMr. Egerton's-opinionas to tbe necessary legislation is diametrically opposed to that of the tenant farmers them- selves? Fellow ,electors, don't be ,hoodwinked by his "extreme dissatisfaction" that Her Majesty's Speech con- tains no allusion to the distress under which the great agri- cultural interest has suffered for the last eight years. It would be much more to the point if he expressed "extreme dissatisfaction," that 'the exaction and tyranny of Tory landlords had rendered it impossible for tenant farmers to live through such unfavourable seasons as have latterly come upon us. It is clear that with the Hon. Alan Egerton as our representative we shall contribute nothing to the wis- dom of the British Parliament. But if we elect Geo. Wm. Latham, we shall send to the councils of the nation one who is looked up to as an authority on 'the land laws, and who has for years been in the vanguard of progress and liberty. Let us, then, remember Latham at the polling booth.—l am, yours sincerely, AN 45INDEPENDENT ELECTOR. March 28th, 1883. LIBERAL MEETING AT HALTON.

, List night a meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. G. W. Latham was held in the Old Court room of the Castle, under the presidency of Mr. John Yapp. There was a large audience, among whom were several tenant farmers, and there were present from Runcorn Messrs. R. Shaw, W. Handley, James Handley, T. Handley, J. R. Frith, B. Kniveton, and 0. Leak. The CHAIRMAN said they were assembled there that even- ing for the purpose of supporting their esteemed friend and neighbour Mr. G. W. Latham, who had for the third time been unanimously chosen to contest this division in the Liberal interest. Few words of his were necessary to explain the cause which he represented, the cause of liberty .against oppression, of progrossion against retro- gression, of retrenchment angainst extravagance.

div.head: HEARTLESS ECOPEMENT FROM HAYDOCK.
div.p: HEARTLESS ECOPEMENT FROM HAYDOCK.
RUNNING AWAY WITH A BROTHER-IN-LAW.

It has been reported that during the present week an elopement of a most heartless character has taken place from the neighbourhood of Haydock, and the circumstances connected therewith have formed the topic of conversation amongst the villagers. It appears that a few months ago a young married person residing, it is said happily and com- fortably with her husband, a collier, received into her house a married sister from Warrington. The husband of the latter, from some cause or other unexplained, found. it _ _

necessary to retire into the Workhouse' taking with him his two children. Not feeling inclined to follow her lord and master, the wife sought the assistance of her married sister, who as stated was living at Haydock. Evidently with a true sisterly love one sister sympathised with the other in her moments of trial and difficulty, and she persuaded her husband to allow her to reside in the same house with them. Thus the sister

from Warrington was saved the dreaded removal to the "big house," and one would have thought that fact would have led her to repay the kindness shown her by her sister. But from her subsequent actions the only inference is that the reverse was the case. Not in the least deterred or held back by the thought that she had a husband living elsewhere, and that she was the mother of two children' she took a liking for her sister's husband. The familiarity became so marked that the sister-in-law found herself in a condition which only naturally raised the ire and passion of the injured wife. The latter had also two children in the house, but the con- siderations which a husband and father would be expected to manifest did not show themselves in this case. Finding
it was getting "too hot" between the two sisters, the husband finally left—a few days ago—taking with him his sister- in-law.
ST. HELENS CONSERVATIVES AND MR. BRADLAUGII.

AMUSING SPEECHES On Wednesday evening a meeting was held in the As- sembly-room at the Conservative Club, St. Helens, for the purpose of oonsidering the desirability of adopting a petition to Parliament to protest against the course the Government are taking regarding the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh into the House of Commons. There was a small attendance. The chair was occupied by Major NVindus, who was sup- ported on the platform by the Rev. A. A. Nunn, the Rev. W. T. Noble, Mr. C. Culshaw, Mr. J. 0. Swift, Mr. M. Elam- mill, and Mr. Fairana.—Mr. Cur.snLve, at the opening of the meeting, gave a brief account of the various iucidents of the Bradlaugh controversy since that gentleman was elected for Northampton, and asked whether the course pursued by Her Majesty's Government or Her Majesty's Opposition was the manly and straightforward course. He had no doubt in his own mind that the course adopted by Sir Stafford Northcote and the Conservative party was the more manly and straightforward of the two. Some people told them that this question of the oath was a trivial question, but he did not consider it was a trivial question at all. He concluded by moving the following resolution :—" That this meeting views with deep regret the action the Government are takhag regarding the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh into the House of Commons ; and at the same time congratulates the leaders of the Opposition on the manly and straight- forward course they have adopted throughout in this matter, and trust they will persevere in this line of action."— Mr. J. O. Switrr seconded the resolution, and in doing so commented severely on the motives of Mr. John Bright and the legal advisers of the Government in supporting the ad- mission of Mr. Bradlaugh to Parliament. With regard to the Government, he did not think they had done anything which had not been a mistake, but he thought nothing had injured them so much in the eyes of the intelligent God- fearing people of this country as the course they had taken with regard to Mr. Bradlaugh. He thought Mr. Bradlaugh wa,s a man whom no member of the Government—although they had made such efforts to get him into Parliament— would like to touch with the end of a barge-pole— (laughter)—and his only value in their eyes was his vote. —Mr. M. lia:stmme having supported the resolution, it was carried.—Mr. FAIRHAM proposed the next resolution, which was as follows:—" That this meeting cordially adopts the petition against the Bill the Government is introducing into Parliament to secure the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh into the House of Commons, and to nullify the Parliamentary Oaths Act; and that the petition be forwarded to the Right Honourable Sir R. A. Cross with a request that he will present it to the House of Commons." He (Mr. Fairam) felt sure in his own mind that it was the threat of bringing 200,000 men down to Westminster which induced the chicken-hearted ministers to bring in the " iniquitous " bill referred to. He thought that if the bill should pass Queen Victoria would not then be able to hold up the Bible and say to the next Indian prince who should visit this country that that was the secret of England's greatness; and, if they did away with the name of God in the House of Commons, they should have to write upon the Bible the word " Ichabod." The Rev. W. T. NOBLE said he believed that the introduction in the bill formed one of those great crisis in the history of a nation, the issues of which should not be determined until an appeal had been made to the country, and he thought that to make a change of so radical a character without allowing an appeal to the cmstituencies was monstrous tyranny and despotism on the part of the Government. He thought if Mr. Gladstme was not the most arrant hypocrite in England he must be doing violence to his own conecience by intro- ducing the bill. Would that devout, pious man, who, when at home at Hawarden, went every Sunday to the parish church and read the lessons, and was even so devout as to go and hear Mr. Spurgeon preach, would this man after all those indications—external indications at least—of God- liness and piety, lend the whole of his great power to sup- port one of the most outrageous blasphemers of God and and religion in England to-day. After some further animadversions against Mr. Gladstone, and deploring from the bottom of his heart that the Duke of Wellington had passed the Catholic Emancipation Act, Mr. Noble concluded, and the resolution was put to the vote, and carried unanimously.—The Rev. Mr. NUNN next addressed the meeting, in opposition to what he called the " nefarious " measure which was about to be in- troduced by the Government, and drew a distinction between Jews into Parliament and the admission of Atheists, much to the advantage of the former. Although, he added, of Jewish descent himself, if the matter had rested with him he would not have admitted Jews to Parliament, though at the same time he would much rather have admitted Jews than Roman Catholics.—At the conclusion of Mr. Nunn's speech, the meeting terminated.

Buckton, Esq. ; hon. secretary, Joseph Davies, Esq.; house-surgeon, Mr. C. E. Richmond. The House Surgeon will feel obliged for con- tributions of old linen, dm. Honorary surgeon for the week, Mr. Joseph. PADGATE WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY: CHARLES LAMB, HUMORIST, diC. Last Thursday, Mr. Elijah Ford delivered a public lecture on the above subject, the chair being taken by Mr. William Bennett. After giving a brief sketch of the earlier life of Lamb, of his term of ser- vice under the East India Company, and his literary labours and associates, among whom were many of the most eminent men of the day, including Coleridge, the poet, Mr. Ford quoted §eme of his poems, which betrayed beneath all their humour something of true pathos, and read extracts from his " Essays of Elia," which were rich in wit and genial satire on the manners of his time, and revealed a pro- found knowledge of human nature, comparing in many respects with some of the *ritings of Dickens. The lecturer then touchingly referred to the gPeat shadow which darkened the life of Lamb, namely, the insanity which at times afflicted his sister, and spoke of the deep affection with which he ever regarded her, in spite of the terrible household tragedy of which she during a temporary aberration of intellect, had been the unwitting instrument. Lamb was a thoroughly genial and warm- hearted philosopher, and though he sometimes startled strangers by his eccentricities, all who were intimate with him regarded him with real esteem. There were flaws in his character which could not be overlooked, but the love which be unceasingly manifested towards his afflicted sister was one of the most beautiful incidents in the history of the world of letters, and atoned in a large measure for his fail- ings. The lecture was enlivened by numerous amusing anecdotes of Lamb, and was delivered in Mr. Ford's most humorous style.—On the motion of Mr. Andrew Rathbone, seconded by Mr. Frederick Wright, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded him, and a similar compliment having been I paid the chairman, the meeting separated.

LATEST NEWS. Yesterday morning, about nine o'clock, a shocking acci- dent occurred at the Barrow Collieries, near Barnsley, resulting in the death of one man and injuries to another. Two miners named Thomas Snee, 26 (single), residing in New-street, Barnsley, and John Winder, of Quarry-street, Barnsley, were workirr, together when a large fall of roof occurred, which killed Snee on the spot, and seriously in- jured the other man. At Gravesend, yesterday, Joseph Hargreaves and James Henry Nuttall, two young men, strangers to the town, were remanded on a charge of presenting a loaded revolver at the sentry of the Kew Tavern Fort. It was contended for the defence that all the parties had been drinking to- gether, and that the complainant drew and flourished his sword. Defendants denied any intention of using the revolvers. THE IRISH CONSPIRACY. EXPECTED ARREST OF "NO. 1." The London correspondent of the Freeman says he is in a position to state that a warrant has been issued for the apprehension of "No. 1," and that copies have been for- warded from Dublin to London, Liverpool, and Birmingham. The man whom the police believe to be "No. 1," will arrive in Dublin on Saturday morning in custody. "No. 1" is not at all a military-looking individual. He is about 45 years of age, of dark complexion, wearing whiskers and moustache, rather tall, and did not occupy during recent years any important position either politically or socially. Mr. Gray, M.P., writes to explain that his temporary absence from the House results from an attack of asthma. A boiler explosion hasoccurred at Ryhope Colliery, doing great damage. No personal 'injury was caused. The writ for the election of a member for Wycombe, in the room of Colonel Carrington. was received by the mayor of the borough yesterday morning, and the nomination is fixed for Wednesday next, and the potting, if any, for the following Saturday. .Mr. JUstice North, at the Old Bailey, yesterday, re- fused an application to admit to bail Henry Arthur Kemp, the publisher, one of the defendants in the 13Yethinker. case.

HOUSE OF LORDS. Earl GRANVILLE, replying to a question, said Lord DO- ferin's despatch on the re-organization of Egypt would be presented immediately the revised copy was received, from his lordship. He (Lord Granville) had telegraphed to Lord Dufferin asking that as little delay as possible might take place prior to its return. Their Lordships then ad-- journed. HOUSE OF COMMONS. . NOTICES or MOTION.—Mr. ARNOLD 'gave notice that on an early day he should move resolutions in favour of uniformity of franchise, and a better representation of the electoral body.—Mr. Cenci gave notice that on an early day he would move a resolution in favour of discontinuing the practice of voting an address to the Crown on the opening of Parliament, as it had become a hindrance to public busi- ness. THE ARMY ESTIMATEL—Lord HARTINOTON, replying to Sir W. Bartelot, said it was proposed to take the army esti- mates next Thursday. COMPULSORY EDUCATION IN IRELAND.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply, Mr. O'SHAUGNESSY. moved that it was expedient to introduce into Ireland the principle of compulsory education, with such modifications as the social and religious conditions of the country required. He said his chief object in moving the resolution was to secure the regular attendance of scholars in schools in Ireland; but that, be felt, would never be achieved until they had powers t 9 enforce attendance. Lord LYMINOTON seconded the resolution, and said its adoption would not cause any serious addition to the burdens of the taxpayers. —Mr. KING. HA.UMAN warmly supported the resolution, and expressed surprise that there were not a greater number of Irish members present to do the same.— [LEFT MTTING.]
